name: Block on a bench spring
statement: A $0.50\ \mathrm{kg}$ block slides on a frictionless bench, attached to a spring of stiffness $k = 200\ \mathrm{N/m}$. The block is pulled aside and released. Find the period of the oscillation in seconds.
solution: The period of a spring-block oscillator is $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$. With $m = 0.50\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $k = 200\ \mathrm{N/m}$, $T = 2\pi\sqrt{0.0025} = 0.314\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Stiffness of a hanging spring
statement: A grocery scale spring stretches $12\ \mathrm{cm}$ when a $0.80\ \mathrm{kg}$ bag hangs at rest from it. Find the spring constant in N/m. Use $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: At rest the spring force balances gravity, so $kx = mg$. Then $k = (0.80)(9.8)/0.12 = 65.3\ \mathrm{N/m}$.

name: Maximum speed of a shaker table
statement: A laboratory shaker table moves in SHM with amplitude $8.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ at a frequency of $2.5\ \mathrm{Hz}$. Find the maximum speed of the table in m/s.
solution: In SHM the speed peaks at $v_{\max} = \omega A$ with $\omega = 2\pi f$. Here $\omega = 2\pi(2.5) = 15.71\ \mathrm{rad/s}$, so $v_{\max} = (15.71)(0.080) = 1.26\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Peak acceleration of a speaker cone
statement: A speaker cone oscillates in SHM with period $0.40\ \mathrm{s}$ and amplitude $2.5\ \mathrm{cm}$. Find the magnitude of its maximum acceleration in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: Maximum acceleration is $a_{\max} = \omega^2 A$ with $\omega = 2\pi/T = 15.71\ \mathrm{rad/s}$. So $a_{\max} = (15.71)^2(0.025) = 6.17\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Stiffness from a measured period
statement: A $1.20\ \mathrm{kg}$ tool box rests on a frictionless air track between the end wall and a spring. When nudged it oscillates with a period of $0.90\ \mathrm{s}$. Find the spring constant in N/m.
solution: Invert $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$ to get $k = 4\pi^2 m/T^2$. With $m = 1.20\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $T = 0.90\ \mathrm{s}$, $k = 4\pi^2(1.20)/0.81 = 58.5\ \mathrm{N/m}$.

name: Energy stored in an oscillator
statement: A block on a spring of stiffness $350\ \mathrm{N/m}$ oscillates with amplitude $6.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ on a frictionless surface. Find the total mechanical energy of the oscillation in joules.
solution: All the energy is elastic at maximum displacement, so $E = \tfrac{1}{2}kA^2$. Then $E = \tfrac{1}{2}(350)(0.060)^2 = 0.630\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Two springs pulling together
statement: A $3.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ cart on a frictionless track is attached to two parallel springs that stretch and compress together, with stiffnesses $120\ \mathrm{N/m}$ and $180\ \mathrm{N/m}$. Find the oscillation frequency in Hz.
solution: Springs that share the same displacement add: $k_{\text{eff}} = 120 + 180 = 300\ \mathrm{N/m}$. Then $f = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{k_{\text{eff}}/m} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{100} = 1.59\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

name: Springs joined end to end
statement: A $2.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ block hangs from a spring of stiffness $400\ \mathrm{N/m}$ that is joined end to end with a second spring of stiffness $600\ \mathrm{N/m}$. Find the period of small vertical oscillations in seconds.
solution: Springs in series share the load, so $1/k_{\text{eff}} = 1/400 + 1/600$, giving $k_{\text{eff}} = 240\ \mathrm{N/m}$. Then $T = 2\pi\sqrt{2.5/240} = 0.641\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Speed halfway out
statement: A $0.90\ \mathrm{kg}$ block on a spring of stiffness $500\ \mathrm{N/m}$ oscillates with amplitude $10.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ on a frictionless surface. Find its speed when it is $5.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ from equilibrium, in m/s.
solution: Energy conservation gives $v = \omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2}$ with $\omega = \sqrt{k/m} = 23.57\ \mathrm{rad/s}$. Then $v = 23.57\sqrt{0.10^2 - 0.05^2} = 2.04\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Car suspension bounce
statement: One corner of a car carries $320\ \mathrm{kg}$ on a suspension spring of stiffness $22000\ \mathrm{N/m}$. Ignoring the shock absorber, find the bounce frequency of that corner in Hz.
solution: Each corner behaves as a mass on a spring, so $f = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{k/m}$. With $k = 22000\ \mathrm{N/m}$ and $m = 320\ \mathrm{kg}$, $f = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{68.75} = 1.32\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

name: Period from the static sag
statement: A hanging spring sags $4.5\ \mathrm{cm}$ when a lamp is hung from it. The lamp is pulled down slightly and released. Find the period of the resulting vertical oscillation in seconds. Use $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: The static sag satisfies $kd = mg$, so $m/k = d/g$ and the mass cancels: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{d/g}$. With $d = 0.045\ \mathrm{m}$, $T = 2\pi\sqrt{0.045/9.8} = 0.426\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Time to fall to half amplitude
statement: A block oscillates with period $0.72\ \mathrm{s}$. It is released from rest at maximum displacement $A$. Find the time in seconds until it first reaches displacement $A/2$.
solution: Take $x = A\cos(\omega t)$. Then $x = A/2$ when $\omega t = \pi/3$, i.e. $t = T/6$. With $T = 0.72\ \mathrm{s}$, $t = 0.120\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Amplitude from a kick
statement: A $1.6\ \mathrm{kg}$ glider on a spring of stiffness $250\ \mathrm{N/m}$ is held $4.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ from equilibrium and then given a push of $0.75\ \mathrm{m/s}$ directly away from equilibrium. Find the amplitude of the resulting oscillation in meters.
solution: Amplitude follows from $A^2 = x_0^2 + (v_0/\omega)^2$ with $\omega = \sqrt{250/1.6} = 12.5\ \mathrm{rad/s}$. Then $A = \sqrt{0.040^2 + (0.75/12.5)^2} = 0.0721\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Half a spring
statement: A block hanging from a spring oscillates with period $0.86\ \mathrm{s}$. The spring is cut exactly in half and the same block is hung from one of the halves. Find the new period in seconds.
solution: Halving a spring's length doubles its stiffness, since each half stretches only half as much under the same force. Then $T \propto 1/\sqrt{k}$ gives $T' = T/\sqrt{2} = 0.86/\sqrt{2} = 0.608\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Coin on a shaking block
statement: A $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ block on a frictionless table is attached to a spring of stiffness $140\ \mathrm{N/m}$. A $0.50\ \mathrm{kg}$ book rests on top of the block, with coefficient of static friction $0.35$ between them. Find the largest amplitude in meters for which the book does not slide. Use $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: Friction alone must supply the book's acceleration, so $\mu g \ge \omega^2 A$ with $\omega^2 = k/(M+m) = 140/2.5 = 56\ \mathrm{s^{-2}}$. Then $A_{\max} = (0.35)(9.8)/56 = 0.0613\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Putty dropped on a glider
statement: A $0.80\ \mathrm{kg}$ glider on a spring of stiffness $180\ \mathrm{N/m}$ oscillates horizontally with amplitude $15.0\ \mathrm{cm}$. As the glider passes through equilibrium, a $0.20\ \mathrm{kg}$ lump of putty is dropped straight down onto it and sticks. Find the new amplitude in meters.
solution: Horizontal momentum is conserved during the drop: $v' = v\,m_1/(m_1+m_2)$ where $v = A\sqrt{k/m_1} = 2.250\ \mathrm{m/s}$, so $v' = 1.800\ \mathrm{m/s}$. The putty passes through equilibrium, so $A' = v'/\omega'$ with $\omega' = \sqrt{180/1.0} = 13.42\ \mathrm{rad/s}$, giving $A' = 0.134\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Time spent near the middle
statement: An oscillator moves in SHM with amplitude $A$. Find the fraction of each full period during which its displacement satisfies $|x| < A/2$. Answer as a dimensionless fraction.
solution: Write $x = A\sin(\omega t)$. Starting from $x=0$, the oscillator reaches $A/2$ at $\omega t = \pi/6$, and by symmetry the condition $|x|<A/2$ holds for four such intervals per period. The fraction is $4(\pi/6)/(2\pi) = 1/3 = 0.333$.

name: Where the energy splits evenly
statement: A block on a spring oscillates with amplitude $12.0\ \mathrm{cm}$. Find the displacement from equilibrium, in meters, at which its kinetic and potential energies are equal.
solution: Setting $\tfrac{1}{2}kx^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(\tfrac{1}{2}kA^2\right)$ gives $x = A/\sqrt{2}$. With $A = 0.12\ \mathrm{m}$, $x = 0.0849\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Pogo stick spring
statement: A $62\ \mathrm{kg}$ rider bounces on a pogo stick, staying in contact with the spring and completing one full bounce cycle every $0.55\ \mathrm{s}$. Treating the rider plus spring as a mass-spring oscillator, find the spring constant in N/m.
solution: The bounce is SHM about the compressed equilibrium point, so $k = 4\pi^2 m/T^2$. With $m = 62\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $T = 0.55\ \mathrm{s}$, $k = 4\pi^2(62)/0.3025 = 8091\ \mathrm{N/m}$.

name: Bobbing wooden buoy
statement: A cylindrical wooden buoy of height $25\ \mathrm{cm}$ and density $650\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$ floats upright in water of density $1000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$. It is pushed down slightly and released. Find the period of the bobbing motion in seconds. Use $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: Pushing the buoy down by $x$ adds a restoring force $\rho_w A g x$, so the effective stiffness is $\rho_w A g$ and $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\rho_b H/(\rho_w g)}$ since $m = \rho_b A H$. Numerically $T = 2\pi\sqrt{(650)(0.25)/(1000\cdot 9.8)} = 0.809\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Cut into thirds, used in pairs
statement: A spring of stiffness $600\ \mathrm{N/m}$ is cut into three equal pieces. Two of the pieces are mounted side by side so they act in parallel on a $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ block on a frictionless table. Find the oscillation frequency in Hz.
solution: Each third has stiffness $3(600) = 1800\ \mathrm{N/m}$, and two in parallel give $3600\ \mathrm{N/m}$. Then $f = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{3600/2.0} = 6.75\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

name: Frequency from one data point
statement: A sensor on an oscillating platform reads an acceleration of $12.0\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ directed toward equilibrium at the instant the platform is $3.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ from equilibrium. Find the oscillation frequency in Hz.
solution: SHM obeys $a = -\omega^2 x$, so $\omega^2 = 12.0/0.030 = 400\ \mathrm{s^{-2}}$ and $\omega = 20\ \mathrm{rad/s}$. Then $f = \omega/2\pi = 3.18\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

name: A spring that is not massless
statement: A $0.40\ \mathrm{kg}$ block oscillates on a horizontal spring of stiffness $160\ \mathrm{N/m}$ whose own mass is $0.30\ \mathrm{kg}$. Accounting for the spring's inertia, find the period of oscillation in seconds.
solution: A uniform spring's coils move with speed proportional to their distance from the fixed end, and integrating the kinetic energy gives an effective added mass of $m_s/3$. So $T = 2\pi\sqrt{(m + m_s/3)/k} = 2\pi\sqrt{0.50/160} = 0.351\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Released at the natural length
statement: A $1.10\ \mathrm{kg}$ mass is attached to an unstretched vertical spring of stiffness $95\ \mathrm{N/m}$ and released from rest. Find the maximum speed it reaches on the way down, in m/s. Use $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: The motion is SHM about the equilibrium point $x_0 = mg/k = 0.1135\ \mathrm{m}$ below the release point, so the amplitude equals $x_0$. Maximum speed is $v = \omega A = \sqrt{k/m}\,(mg/k) = 0.1135\sqrt{95/1.10} = 1.055\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Bouncing between two springs
statement: A $1.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ puck slides on a frictionless track between two springs that it touches but is not attached to, of stiffness $300\ \mathrm{N/m}$ on the left and $800\ \mathrm{N/m}$ on the right. The puck is always in contact with one spring or the other. Find the period of the motion in seconds.
solution: The puck executes half a cycle against each spring, and each half-cycle takes $\pi\sqrt{m/k}$ for that spring. So $T = \pi\sqrt{1.5/300} + \pi\sqrt{1.5/800} = 0.2221 + 0.1360 = 0.358\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Book on a vibrating platform
statement: A $0.85\ \mathrm{kg}$ book rests on a horizontal platform supported by a vertical spring of stiffness $240\ \mathrm{N/m}$; the platform's own mass is negligible. The system oscillates vertically. Find the largest amplitude in meters for which the book stays in contact with the platform. Use $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: Contact is lost when the platform's downward acceleration at the top of the motion exceeds $g$, so the condition is $\omega^2 A \le g$ with $\omega^2 = k/m = 240/0.85 = 282.4\ \mathrm{s^{-2}}$. Then $A_{\max} = 9.8/282.4 = 0.0347\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Package dropped onto a spring scale
statement: A $3.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ package is dropped from a height of $25\ \mathrm{cm}$ onto the massless pan of a spring scale of stiffness $1200\ \mathrm{N/m}$, and it stays on the pan. Find the amplitude of the resulting oscillation in meters. Use $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: After landing the motion is SHM about the new equilibrium $x_0 = mg/k = 0.0245\ \mathrm{m}$ below the pan's original position. At contact the displacement from that center is $x_0$ and the speed is $\sqrt{2gh}$, so $A = \sqrt{x_0^2 + 2mgh/k} = \sqrt{6.0\times10^{-4} + 1.225\times10^{-2}} = 0.1134\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Mass on a movable pulley
statement: A light string has one end fixed to the ceiling and the other end attached to a spring of stiffness $900\ \mathrm{N/m}$ that also hangs from the ceiling. The string passes under a frictionless massless pulley from which a $5.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ mass hangs. Find the period of vertical oscillation of the mass in seconds.
solution: If the mass descends by $x$, the pulley lets out $2x$ of string, so the spring stretches $2x$ and its tension rises by $2kx$. That tension appears in both string segments supporting the pulley only through the single spring end, so the net upward force on the mass changes by $kx/2$: the effective stiffness is $k/4$. Hence $T = 2\pi\sqrt{4m/k} = 2\pi\sqrt{20/900} = 0.937\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Two carts joined by a spring
statement: Two carts of mass $0.60\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $0.90\ \mathrm{kg}$ are joined by a spring of stiffness $320\ \mathrm{N/m}$ and released on a frictionless horizontal track with the spring stretched. Find the frequency of the resulting oscillation in Hz.
solution: In the center-of-mass frame the separation coordinate obeys SHM with the reduced mass $\mu = m_1m_2/(m_1+m_2) = 0.36\ \mathrm{kg}$. Then $f = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{k/\mu} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{888.9} = 4.75\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

name: Rolling cylinder on a spring
statement: A solid cylinder of mass $1.8\ \mathrm{kg}$ rolls without slipping on a level floor. A horizontal spring of stiffness $250\ \mathrm{N/m}$ connects the wall to a frictionless collar on the cylinder's axle, so the spring force acts at the center. Find the period of small oscillations in seconds.
solution: With rolling, the kinetic energy is $\tfrac{1}{2}Mv^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}(\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2)(v/R)^2 = \tfrac{3}{4}Mv^2$, so the effective mass is $\tfrac{3}{2}M$. Then $T = 2\pi\sqrt{3M/(2k)} = 2\pi\sqrt{5.4/500} = 0.653\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: One-meter pendulum
statement: A small brass bob hangs from a light string of length $1.00\ \mathrm{m}$ and swings through a small angle. Find the period in seconds. Use $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: For small swings $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$. With $L = 1.00\ \mathrm{m}$ and $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, $T = 2\pi\sqrt{0.10204} = 2.007\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Seconds pendulum
statement: A clock pendulum is to have a period of exactly $2.00\ \mathrm{s}$, so that each swing takes one second. Find the required length in meters. Use $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: Solve $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$ for $L = gT^2/4\pi^2$. With $T = 2.00\ \mathrm{s}$, $L = 9.8(4)/39.478 = 0.9930\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Pendulum on the Moon
statement: An astronaut sets up a $0.60\ \mathrm{m}$ pendulum on the Moon, where $g = 1.62\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Find its period in seconds.
solution: Use $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$ with the local gravity. Then $T = 2\pi\sqrt{0.60/1.62} = 3.82\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Frequency of a short pendulum
statement: A pendulum in a wall clock has length $25\ \mathrm{cm}$. Find its frequency of small oscillation in Hz. Use $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: The frequency is $f = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{g/L} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{39.2} = 0.997\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

name: Swings per minute
statement: A $0.45\ \mathrm{m}$ pendulum swings with small amplitude. Find the number of complete oscillations it makes in $60\ \mathrm{s}$. Use $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: The period is $T = 2\pi\sqrt{0.45/9.8} = 1.346\ \mathrm{s}$. The number of cycles in one minute is $60/T = 44.6$.

name: Doubling the length
statement: A pendulum has a period of $1.55\ \mathrm{s}$. Its string is replaced with one twice as long. Find the new period in seconds.
solution: Since $T \propto \sqrt{L}$, doubling the length multiplies the period by $\sqrt{2}$. So $T' = 1.55\sqrt{2} = 2.19\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Swinging rod
statement: A uniform rod of length $0.80\ \mathrm{m}$ hangs from a frictionless pivot at one end and swings through a small angle. Find its period in seconds. Use $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: For a rod pivoted at its end, $I = \tfrac{1}{3}mL^2$ and the center of mass is at $L/2$, so $T = 2\pi\sqrt{I/(mgd)} = 2\pi\sqrt{2L/3g}$. Then $T = 2\pi\sqrt{1.6/29.4} = 1.466\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Torsional balance wheel
statement: A balance wheel with moment of inertia $4.0\times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}$ is suspended from a wire with torsional constant $0.025\ \mathrm{N\,m/rad}$. Find the period of torsional oscillation in seconds.
solution: A torsional pendulum obeys $\tau = -\kappa\theta$, giving $T = 2\pi\sqrt{I/\kappa}$. Then $T = 2\pi\sqrt{0.0040/0.025} = 2.51\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Speed at the bottom
statement: A pendulum bob on a $1.20\ \mathrm{m}$ string is pulled aside until the string makes $8.0^\circ$ with the vertical and released. Find the bob's speed at the lowest point in m/s. Use $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: The bob drops a height $h = L(1-\cos\theta_0) = 1.20(1-\cos 8^\circ) = 0.01168\ \mathrm{m}$. Energy conservation gives $v = \sqrt{2gh} = 0.478\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Measuring g
statement: A student times a $0.750\ \mathrm{m}$ pendulum and finds a period of $1.74\ \mathrm{s}$. Find the value of $g$ implied by this measurement, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: Rearrange $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$ to $g = 4\pi^2 L/T^2$. Then $g = 4\pi^2(0.750)/(1.74)^2 = 9.78\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Adjusting a slow clock
statement: A pendulum clock keeps correct time when its pendulum has period $2.000\ \mathrm{s}$, but it currently runs slow with a period of $2.008\ \mathrm{s}$. Find how much the pendulum must be shortened, in millimeters. Use $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: Length scales as $L = gT^2/4\pi^2$. The slow clock is too long by $\Delta L = g(T_2^2 - T_1^2)/4\pi^2 = 9.8(2.008^2-2.000^2)/(4\pi^2) = 7.96\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}$, so $7.96\ \mathrm{mm}$ must be removed.

name: Pendulum in a rising elevator
statement: A $0.90\ \mathrm{m}$ pendulum hangs in an elevator that accelerates upward at $2.5\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Find its period of small oscillation in seconds. Use $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: In the accelerating frame the effective gravity is $g + a = 12.3\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Then $T = 2\pi\sqrt{0.90/12.3} = 1.700\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Pendulum in an accelerating car
statement: A $0.55\ \mathrm{m}$ pendulum hangs from the roof of a car that accelerates horizontally at $3.0\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ on a straight road. Find its period of small oscillation about the new equilibrium direction, in seconds. Use $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: In the car's frame gravity and the pseudo-force combine into $g_{\text{eff}} = \sqrt{g^2+a^2} = \sqrt{96.04+9} = 10.25\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, tilted from vertical. The period is $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g_{\text{eff}}} = 1.455\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Disk on a nail
statement: A uniform disk of radius $22\ \mathrm{cm}$ hangs on a horizontal nail through a small hole at its rim and swings in its own plane. Find the period of small oscillations in seconds. Use $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: About the rim, $I = \tfrac{1}{2}mR^2 + mR^2 = \tfrac{3}{2}mR^2$ and $d = R$, so $T = 2\pi\sqrt{3R/2g}$. Then $T = 2\pi\sqrt{0.66/19.6} = 1.153\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Bicycle tire on a peg
statement: A bicycle tire of radius $31\ \mathrm{cm}$, treated as a thin hoop, hangs on a horizontal peg at its rim and swings in its own plane. Find the period of small oscillations in seconds. Use $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: For a hoop about a rim point, $I = mR^2 + mR^2 = 2mR^2$ and $d = R$, so $T = 2\pi\sqrt{2R/g}$. Then $T = 2\pi\sqrt{0.62/9.8} = 1.581\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Torsion constant of a wire
statement: A uniform disk of mass $0.40\ \mathrm{kg}$ and radius $9.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ hangs horizontally from a vertical wire attached at its center. Twisted slightly, it oscillates with period $1.90\ \mathrm{s}$. Find the torsional constant of the wire in $\mathrm{N\,m/rad}$.
solution: The disk's moment of inertia is $I = \tfrac{1}{2}mR^2 = 1.62\times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}$. From $T = 2\pi\sqrt{I/\kappa}$, $\kappa = 4\pi^2 I/T^2 = 1.77\times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{N\,m/rad}$.

name: Rod with a weight at the end
statement: A uniform rod of mass $0.50\ \mathrm{kg}$ and length $1.00\ \mathrm{m}$ is pivoted at one end, and a compact $0.80\ \mathrm{kg}$ weight is fastened at the far end. Find the period of small oscillations in seconds. Use $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: Add the contributions: $I = \tfrac{1}{3}m_rL^2 + ML^2 = 0.9667\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}$, and the center of mass sits at $d = (m_rL/2 + ML)/(m_r+M) = 0.8077\ \mathrm{m}$. Then $T = 2\pi\sqrt{I/((m_r+M)gd)} = 1.926\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Clock carried up a mountain
statement: A pendulum clock that keeps perfect time at sea level is carried to a mountain observatory $3000\ \mathrm{m}$ higher. Taking Earth's radius as $6371\ \mathrm{km}$ and $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ at sea level, find how many seconds the clock loses per day.
solution: Gravity falls as $g' = g(R/(R+h))^2$, and the period grows as $T \propto 1/\sqrt{g}$, so the clock runs slow by a fraction $1 - \sqrt{g'/g} \approx h/R$. Per day the loss is $86400(1-\sqrt{g'/g}) = 40.7\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: String tension at the bottom
statement: A $0.70\ \mathrm{kg}$ pendulum bob is released from rest with the string $25^\circ$ from vertical. Find the string tension as the bob passes through the lowest point, in newtons. Use $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: Energy gives $v^2 = 2gL(1-\cos\theta_0)$, and at the bottom $T - mg = mv^2/L$, so $T = mg(3 - 2\cos\theta_0)$. With $\theta_0 = 25^\circ$, $T = 0.70(9.8)(3-1.8126) = 8.15\ \mathrm{N}$.

name: Clock in a hot room
statement: A pendulum clock with a brass rod (linear expansion coefficient $1.9\times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}$) is calibrated at $2\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and then used in a room at $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Find how many seconds it loses per day.
solution: The rod lengthens by a fraction $\alpha\Delta T$, and since $T \propto \sqrt{L}$ the period grows by $\tfrac{1}{2}\alpha\Delta T$. Over a day the loss is $86400\cdot\tfrac{1}{2}(1.9\times10^{-5})(18) = 14.8\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Pendulum caught by a peg
statement: A pendulum of length $1.20\ \mathrm{m}$ hangs from a pivot, and a peg is fixed $0.50\ \mathrm{m}$ directly below the pivot. On each swing to one side the string catches on the peg, shortening the pendulum. Find the period of the full motion in seconds. Use $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: Each side of the swing is half a cycle of a pendulum of the appropriate length: $\pi\sqrt{L/g}$. With $L_1 = 1.20\ \mathrm{m}$ and $L_2 = 0.70\ \mathrm{m}$, $T = \pi\sqrt{1.20/9.8} + \pi\sqrt{0.70/9.8} = 1.0997 + 0.8398 = 1.939\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Hanging angle in a braking train
statement: A cord with a small weight hangs from the ceiling of a train car that is braking at $4.2\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Find the angle between the cord and the vertical at equilibrium, in degrees. Use $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: In the train's frame the weight hangs along the effective gravity, which is tilted by $\theta = \arctan(a/g)$. So $\theta = \arctan(4.2/9.8) = 23.2^\circ$.

name: Center of oscillation of a rod
statement: A uniform rod of length $1.20\ \mathrm{m}$ swings about a horizontal pivot located $0.40\ \mathrm{m}$ from its center. Find the distance from the pivot to the center of oscillation (the length of the equivalent simple pendulum), in meters.
solution: The equivalent simple length is $\ell = I/(md) = (L^2/12 + d^2)/d$. With $L = 1.20\ \mathrm{m}$ and $d = 0.40\ \mathrm{m}$, $\ell = (0.12 + 0.16)/0.40 = 0.700\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Fastest swinging rod
statement: A uniform rod of length $1.00\ \mathrm{m}$ has a hole drilled at a distance $d$ from its center and is hung on a nail through the hole. The position of the hole is chosen to make the period as short as possible. Find that minimum period in seconds. Use $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: The period is $T = 2\pi\sqrt{(L^2/12 + d^2)/(gd)}$; minimizing over $d$ gives $d = L/\sqrt{12} = 0.2887\ \mathrm{m}$, where the two terms are equal. Substituting, $T_{\min} = 2\pi\sqrt{2d/g} = 2\pi\sqrt{0.05892} = 1.525\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Meter stick on a pin
statement: A uniform meter stick is pivoted on a pin through the $20\ \mathrm{cm}$ mark and swings in a vertical plane. Find the period of small oscillations in seconds. Use $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: The pivot is $d = 0.30\ \mathrm{m}$ from the center, and $I = m(L^2/12 + d^2)$. Then $T = 2\pi\sqrt{(0.08333+0.09)/(9.8\cdot 0.30)} = 1.526\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Pendulum on a sliding cart
statement: A cart slides freely down a frictionless $30^\circ$ incline. A $0.65\ \mathrm{m}$ pendulum hangs from the cart's roof. Find the period of small oscillations of the pendulum in seconds. Use $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: In the cart's frame the pseudo-force cancels the component of gravity along the incline, leaving only the perpendicular component $g\cos\theta = 8.487\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Then $T = 2\pi\sqrt{0.65/8.487} = 1.739\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Unknown body on a torsion wire
statement: A uniform disk of mass $0.60\ \mathrm{kg}$ and radius $12\ \mathrm{cm}$ hangs from a torsion wire and oscillates with period $1.60\ \mathrm{s}$. An irregular object is then clamped on top of the disk, sharing the same axis, and the period becomes $2.30\ \mathrm{s}$. Find the object's moment of inertia about that axis in $\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$.
solution: Since $T^2 \propto I$ with the same wire, $I_2/I_1 = (T_2/T_1)^2$. With $I_1 = \tfrac{1}{2}(0.60)(0.12)^2 = 4.32\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}$, the added inertia is $I_1[(2.30/1.60)^2 - 1] = 4.61\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}$.

name: Pendulum with a real bob
statement: A pendulum consists of a solid sphere of radius $5.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ hung so that its center is $0.900\ \mathrm{m}$ below the pivot on a light rod. Find the period of small oscillations in seconds. Use $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: The sphere spins as it swings, so $I = m(L^2 + \tfrac{2}{5}r^2)$ about the pivot, while the restoring torque still uses $d = L$. Then $T = 2\pi\sqrt{(L^2 + 0.4r^2)/(gL)} = 2\pi\sqrt{0.811/8.82} = 1.9053\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Swinging too far
statement: A pendulum of length $1.00\ \mathrm{m}$ is released from rest at $30.0^\circ$ from the vertical, an angle too large for the small-angle formula. Using the expansion $T = T_0\left(1 + \frac{\theta_0^2}{16} + \frac{11\theta_0^4}{3072}\right)$ with $\theta_0$ in radians, find the period in seconds. Use $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: The small-angle period is $T_0 = 2\pi\sqrt{1.00/9.8} = 2.0071\ \mathrm{s}$, and $\theta_0 = 0.5236\ \mathrm{rad}$. The correction factor is $1 + 0.017135 + 0.000269 = 1.017404$, giving $T = 2.042\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Rod and disk pendulum
statement: A uniform rod of mass $0.60\ \mathrm{kg}$ and length $1.00\ \mathrm{m}$ is pivoted at its top end. A uniform disk of mass $1.20\ \mathrm{kg}$ and radius $0.10\ \mathrm{m}$ is rigidly attached to the rod's lower end, in the plane of swing, with the rod meeting the disk at its rim so the disk's center is $1.10\ \mathrm{m}$ from the pivot. Find the period of small oscillations in seconds. Use $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: About the pivot, $I = \tfrac{1}{3}m_rL^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}M R^2 + M(1.10)^2 = 0.2 + 0.006 + 1.452 = 1.658\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}$. The combined center of mass is at $d = (0.60\cdot 0.50 + 1.20\cdot 1.10)/1.80 = 0.900\ \mathrm{m}$. Then $T = 2\pi\sqrt{1.658/(1.80\cdot 9.8\cdot 0.900)} = 2.031\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Glider at maximum speed
statement: A 0.50 kg air-track glider is attached to a spring of stiffness $k = 200$ N/m and oscillates with amplitude $A = 0.10$ m. Friction is negligible. What is the glider's maximum speed, in m/s?
solution: All the energy is spring potential at the turning point and all kinetic at the centre, so $\tfrac12 kA^2 = \tfrac12 m v_{\max}^2$. Thus $v_{\max} = A\sqrt{k/m} = 0.10\sqrt{200/0.50} = 2.0$ m/s.

name: Energy stored in a door-closer spring
statement: A 1.2 kg block on a spring with $k = 350$ N/m oscillates horizontally with amplitude 4.0 cm. What is the total mechanical energy of the oscillation, in J?
solution: The total energy equals the spring potential energy at maximum displacement: $E = \tfrac12 kA^2$. With $A = 0.040$ m, $E = \tfrac12(350)(0.040)^2 = 0.28$ J.

name: Speed at half the amplitude
statement: A 0.25 kg puck on a spring of stiffness 100 N/m swings with amplitude 8.0 cm. What is its speed when it is 4.0 cm from equilibrium, in m/s?
solution: Energy conservation gives $v = \sqrt{(k/m)(A^2-x^2)}$. Here $\sqrt{k/m} = 20$ s$^{-1}$ and $\sqrt{A^2-x^2} = \sqrt{0.080^2-0.040^2} = 0.06928$ m, so $v = 1.386$ m/s.

name: Kinetic fraction at 0.6 A
statement: A mass on a spring oscillates with amplitude $A$. When its displacement is $x = 0.60A$, what fraction of the total mechanical energy is kinetic? Give a pure number.
solution: The potential fraction is $U/E = x^2/A^2 = 0.36$. Everything else is kinetic, so $K/E = 1 - 0.36 = 0.64$.

name: Where kinetic equals potential
statement: A block on a spring oscillates with amplitude 12.0 cm. At what distance from equilibrium is its kinetic energy exactly equal to the spring potential energy? Give the answer in m.
solution: Setting $\tfrac12 kx^2 = \tfrac12 E$ with $E = \tfrac12 kA^2$ gives $x = A/\sqrt2$. Then $x = 0.120/\sqrt2 = 0.08485$ m.

name: Pendulum bob at the bottom
statement: A 0.30 kg bob hangs from a 1.20 m string. It is pulled aside until the string makes $15^\circ$ with the vertical and released from rest. Take $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$. What is the bob's speed at the lowest point, in m/s?
solution: The bob rises $h = L(1-\cos\theta)$ above the lowest point, so $v = \sqrt{2gL(1-\cos 15^\circ)}$. Numerically $h = 1.20(1-0.96593) = 0.04089$ m and $v = 0.8952$ m/s.

name: Average kinetic energy over a cycle
statement: A 0.40 kg mass on a spring with $k = 90$ N/m oscillates with amplitude 5.0 cm. Averaged over one full cycle, what is its kinetic energy, in J?
solution: For SHM the cycle-averaged kinetic and potential energies are equal, each half the total. With $E = \tfrac12(90)(0.050)^2 = 0.1125$ J, the average kinetic energy is $0.05625$ J.

name: Total energy from the maximum speed
statement: A 2.0 kg block on a frictionless horizontal spring reaches a maximum speed of 3.0 m/s. What is the total mechanical energy of the oscillation, in J?
solution: At the centre the energy is entirely kinetic, so $E = \tfrac12 m v_{\max}^2 = \tfrac12(2.0)(3.0)^2 = 9.0$ J.

name: Energy lost to damping
statement: A 0.80 kg block on a spring with $k = 150$ N/m starts with amplitude 10.0 cm. Weak air drag reduces the amplitude to 6.0 cm. How much mechanical energy has been dissipated, in J?
solution: Energy scales as the square of amplitude: $E = \tfrac12 kA^2$. Here $E_i = 0.750$ J and $E_f = 0.270$ J, so $0.480$ J has been lost to drag.

name: Released from rest on a vertical spring
statement: A 1.5 kg mass hangs at rest on a vertical spring of stiffness 45 N/m. It is pulled down 8.0 cm from that equilibrium position and released. What is its maximum speed during the resulting oscillation, in m/s?
solution: Measured from the hanging equilibrium, gravity is already absorbed into the equilibrium shift, so the motion is SHM with amplitude 0.080 m about that point. Then $v_{\max} = A\sqrt{k/m} = 0.080\sqrt{45/1.5} = 0.4382$ m/s.

name: Putty lands at the centre
statement: A 0.60 kg block oscillates on a spring ($k = 240$ N/m) with amplitude 10.0 cm on a frictionless table. As the block passes through equilibrium, a 0.30 kg lump of putty is dropped vertically onto it and sticks. What is the new amplitude, in m?
solution: The vertical drop carries no horizontal momentum, so horizontal momentum is conserved at the centre: $v' = m v/(m+\Delta m)$. With $v = 0.10\sqrt{240/0.60} = 2.0$ m/s, $v' = 1.333$ m/s, and $A' = v'\sqrt{(m+\Delta m)/k} = 0.0816$ m.

name: Putty lands at the turning point
statement: A 0.60 kg block oscillates on a spring ($k = 240$ N/m) with amplitude 10.0 cm on a frictionless table. This time the 0.30 kg lump of putty is dropped onto the block exactly when the block is momentarily at rest at maximum displacement. What is the new maximum speed of the oscillation, in m/s?
solution: The block is at rest when the putty lands, so no energy is lost and the amplitude stays 0.10 m; only the mass changes. Then $v_{\max} = A\sqrt{k/(m+\Delta m)} = 0.10\sqrt{240/0.90} = 1.633$ m/s.

name: Top block lifted off
statement: A 0.50 kg block sits on top of a 0.50 kg block attached to a spring with $k = 120$ N/m; the pair oscillates together with amplitude 6.0 cm. At the instant the system is at maximum displacement, the top block is lifted straight up and removed. What is the maximum speed of the remaining block afterwards, in m/s?
solution: At maximum displacement the speed is zero, so removing the top block changes neither the position nor the stored spring energy: the amplitude stays 0.060 m. The lighter system is faster: $v_{\max} = 0.060\sqrt{120/0.50} = 0.9295$ m/s.

name: Top block removed at the centre
statement: The same 1.00 kg pair of stacked blocks oscillates on the $k = 120$ N/m spring with amplitude 6.0 cm. Now the 0.50 kg top block is lifted off exactly as the system passes through equilibrium, leaving the bottom block's velocity unchanged. What is the new amplitude, in m?
solution: The speed at the centre is unchanged, $v = 0.060\sqrt{120/1.00} = 0.6573$ m/s, but the angular frequency rises to $\sqrt{120/0.50} = 15.49$ s$^{-1}$. The new amplitude is $A' = v/\omega' = 0.04243$ m.

name: Pendulum halfway back
statement: A pendulum of length 1.50 m swings with angular amplitude $20^\circ$. Take $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$. What is the bob's speed when the string makes $10^\circ$ with the vertical, in m/s?
solution: Energy conservation gives $v = \sqrt{2gL(\cos\theta-\cos\theta_0)}$, which is exact for any amplitude. With $\cos 10^\circ - \cos 20^\circ = 0.04511$, $v = \sqrt{2(9.8)(1.50)(0.04511)} = 1.152$ m/s.

name: Amplitude after ten damped cycles
statement: A damped oscillator loses 3.0% of its mechanical energy each cycle. What fraction of its original amplitude remains after 10 cycles? Give a pure number.
solution: Energy after 10 cycles is $(0.97)^{10}E_0$, and amplitude scales as $\sqrt{E}$. So $A_{10}/A_0 = (0.97)^{5} = 0.8587$.

name: Fraction of the period with mostly kinetic energy
statement: A mass undergoes simple harmonic motion. What fraction of each period does it spend in the region where its kinetic energy exceeds three times its potential energy? Give a pure number.
solution: $K > 3U$ means $A^2-x^2 > 3x^2$, i.e. $|x| < A/2$. With $x = A\sin(\omega t)$ the time fraction inside $|x|<A/2$ is $(2/\pi)\arcsin(1/2) = 1/3 = 0.3333$.

name: Dropped from the natural length
statement: A 0.90 kg mass is attached to an unstretched vertical spring of stiffness 60 N/m and released from rest. Take $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$. What is the amplitude of the resulting oscillation, in m?
solution: The equilibrium point is a distance $mg/k$ below the release point, and the mass starts at rest there, so the release point is a turning point and the amplitude is exactly $mg/k$. That gives $A = (0.90)(9.8)/60 = 0.147$ m.

name: Maximum speed of the dropped mass
statement: The same 0.90 kg mass is released from rest on the unstretched 60 N/m vertical spring. What is its maximum speed on the way down, in m/s?
solution: The amplitude about the hanging equilibrium is $A = mg/k = 0.147$ m, so $v_{\max} = A\sqrt{k/m} = 0.147\sqrt{60/0.90} = 1.200$ m/s.

name: Sloshing water in a U-tube
statement: Water fills a U-tube of uniform cross-section; the total length of the water column is 0.80 m. The water is displaced so that one side stands 12 cm above its equilibrium level, then released. Take $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$ and neglect viscosity. What is the maximum speed of the water column, in m/s?
solution: Displacing the column by $x$ raises a slug of height $2x$, giving $U = \rho A g x^2$ and the SHM frequency $\omega = \sqrt{2g/L}$. Then $v_{\max} = A\omega = 0.12\sqrt{2(9.8)/0.80} = 0.5940$ m/s.

name: Amplitude from a kick
statement: A 0.30 kg block on a spring with $k = 75$ N/m is at $x = 5.0$ cm from equilibrium and moving at 0.40 m/s. What is the amplitude of its oscillation, in m?
solution: Total energy is $\tfrac12 kx^2 + \tfrac12 mv^2 = \tfrac12 kA^2$, so $A = \sqrt{x^2 + v^2 m/k}$. With $m/k = 0.004$ s$^2$, $A = \sqrt{0.0025+0.00064} = 0.05604$ m.

name: Half-life of a damped oscillation
statement: A 0.50 kg mass oscillates on a spring with a weak drag force $F = -bv$, $b = 0.040$ kg/s. Its mechanical energy decays as $E(t) = E_0 e^{-bt/m}$. How long does it take for the energy to fall to half its initial value, in s?

name: Counting cycles with sliding friction
statement: A 0.80 kg block on a horizontal surface is attached to a spring with $k = 160$ N/m. The coefficient of kinetic friction is $\mu = 0.20$ and $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$. The block is pulled 15.0 cm from equilibrium and released. How many complete cycles does it perform before it stops permanently? Give an integer count of complete cycles.
solution: Friction removes a fixed amplitude $4\mu mg/k = 0.0392$ m per full cycle. The block sticks once its turning-point displacement falls below $\mu mg/k = 0.0098$ m, so it must lose $0.150-0.0098 = 0.1402$ m of amplitude; $0.1402/0.0392 = 3.58$, giving 3 complete cycles.

name: Total path length before stopping
statement: A 0.50 kg block on a spring with $k = 100$ N/m is released from rest 20.0 cm from equilibrium on a surface with $\mu = 0.25$ and $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$. Ignoring the small residual spring energy at the final resting point, what total distance does the block travel before stopping, in m?
solution: All the initial spring energy goes into friction: $\tfrac12 kA^2 = \mu m g\, d$. With $\tfrac12(100)(0.20)^2 = 2.00$ J and $\mu mg = 1.225$ N, $d = 1.633$ m.

name: Cylinder rolling on a spring
statement: A uniform solid cylinder of mass 0.60 kg and radius 5.0 cm is attached at its axle to a horizontal spring of stiffness 180 N/m and rolls without slipping. It is released from rest with the spring stretched 9.0 cm. What is the maximum speed of the cylinder's centre, in m/s?
solution: Rolling gives kinetic energy $\tfrac12 mv^2 + \tfrac12(\tfrac12 mR^2)(v/R)^2 = \tfrac34 mv^2$, i.e. an effective mass $\tfrac32 m$ independent of $R$. Then $v_{\max} = A\sqrt{k/(1.5m)} = 0.09\sqrt{180/0.90} = 1.273$ m/s.

name: Two masses joined by a spring
statement: Two blocks of mass 0.40 kg and 0.60 kg on a frictionless table are joined by a spring of stiffness 250 N/m. With the centre of mass at rest, the spring is stretched 5.0 cm beyond its natural length and the system is released. What is the maximum relative speed of the two blocks, in m/s?
solution: In the centre-of-mass frame the relative coordinate obeys SHM with reduced mass $\mu = m_1m_2/(m_1+m_2) = 0.24$ kg. Energy conservation gives $v_{\rm rel,max} = A\sqrt{k/\mu} = 0.05\sqrt{250/0.24} = 1.614$ m/s.

name: Energy loss per cycle from Q
statement: A tuning fork oscillator has quality factor $Q = 40$, defined by $E(t) = E_0 e^{-\omega_0 t/Q}$ with $\omega_0$ the natural angular frequency. What fraction of its energy does it lose during one full period of oscillation? Give a pure number.
solution: One period is $T = 2\pi/\omega_0$, so the energy ratio across a period is $e^{-2\pi/Q}$. The fraction lost is $1-e^{-2\pi/40} = 1-0.8546 = 0.1454$.

name: String tension at the bottom of a wide swing
statement: A bob on a 1.00 m string is released from rest with the string at $60^\circ$ from the vertical. At the lowest point, what is the ratio of the string tension to the bob's weight? Give a pure number.
solution: Energy gives $v^2 = 2gL(1-\cos\theta_0)$ at the bottom. Newton's second law there is $T - mg = mv^2/L$, so $T/mg = 1 + 2(1-\cos\theta_0) = 3-2\cos 60^\circ = 2.000$.

name: Slowly leaking sand
statement: A bucket of sand of total mass 1.00 kg hangs from a spring and oscillates vertically. Sand leaks out through a small hole so slowly that many oscillations occur while the mass changes appreciably; the leaking sand carries away no extra energy and the spring is ideal. By what factor does the oscillation amplitude (measured about the instantaneous equilibrium) grow by the time the mass has fallen to 0.25 kg? Give a pure number.
solution: For a slow parameter change the adiabatic invariant $E/\omega$ is conserved. With $E = \tfrac12 kA^2$ and $\omega = \sqrt{k/m}$, $A^2\sqrt{m}$ is constant, so $A \propto m^{-1/4}$. The factor is $(1.00/0.25)^{1/4} = 1.414$.

name: Speed at the centre with friction
statement: A 1.00 kg block on a rough horizontal surface ($\mu = 0.15$, $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$) is attached to a spring with $k = 200$ N/m. It is released from rest 20.0 cm from equilibrium. What is its speed the first time it passes through the equilibrium position, in m/s?
solution: Spring energy minus friction work equals kinetic energy: $\tfrac12 kA^2 - \mu mgA = \tfrac12 mv^2$. Here $4.00 - 0.294 = 3.706$ J, so $v = \sqrt{2(3.706)/1.00} = 2.722$ m/s.

name: Equilibrium of a quadratic potential
statement: A cart moving along a track has potential energy $U(x) = 3x^2 - 12x$, with $U$ in joules and $x$ in metres. At what value of $x$ is the cart in equilibrium? Give the answer in m.
solution: Equilibrium requires $F = -dU/dx = 0$. Here $dU/dx = 6x - 12$, which vanishes at $x = 2.0$ m. Since $U'' = 6 > 0$ this point is a stable minimum.

name: Frequency from the curvature
statement: A 0.20 kg bead slides on a wire where its potential energy is $U(x) = 40x^2$ ($U$ in J, $x$ in m). What is the angular frequency of its oscillation about $x = 0$, in rad/s?
solution: Near a minimum the effective stiffness is $k_{\rm eff} = U''(x_0)$. Here $U'' = 80$ N/m, so $\omega = \sqrt{80/0.20} = 20.0$ rad/s.

name: Marble in a spherical bowl
statement: A small marble slides without friction inside a spherical bowl of radius 0.25 m, staying near the bottom. Take $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$. What is the angular frequency of its small oscillations, in rad/s?
solution: Near the bottom the bowl's surface is $y \approx x^2/2R$, so $U = mgx^2/2R$ and $k_{\rm eff} = mg/R$. The mass cancels: $\omega = \sqrt{g/R} = \sqrt{9.8/0.25} = 6.261$ rad/s.

name: Lennard-Jones bond length
statement: Two argon atoms interact through $U(r) = 4\varepsilon\left[(\sigma/r)^{12} - (\sigma/r)^{6}\right]$ with $\sigma = 0.340$ nm. What is the equilibrium separation of the pair, in nm?

name: Depth of the Lennard-Jones well
statement: For the same argon pair, $\varepsilon = 1.65\times10^{-21}$ J. Starting from rest at the equilibrium separation, what is the minimum energy needed to pull the two atoms infinitely far apart, in J?
solution: At $r_0 = 2^{1/6}\sigma$ the potential takes its minimum value $U(r_0) = -\varepsilon$, and $U \to 0$ as $r \to \infty$. The dissociation energy is therefore exactly $\varepsilon = 1.65\times10^{-21}$ J.

name: Bead on a parabolic wire
statement: A bead slides without friction on a wire bent into the parabola $y = cx^2$ in a vertical plane, with $c = 0.80$ m$^{-1}$ and $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$. What is the angular frequency of its small oscillations about the bottom, in rad/s?
solution: The potential is $U = mgcx^2$, so $U'' = 2mgc$ and $\omega = \sqrt{2gc}$, independent of mass. Numerically $\omega = \sqrt{2(9.8)(0.80)} = 3.96$ rad/s.

name: Equilibrium of a hanging mass
statement: A 0.75 kg mass hangs on a vertical spring of stiffness 60 N/m. Measuring $x$ downward from the unstretched position, $U(x) = \tfrac12 kx^2 - mgx$. Take $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$. How far below the unstretched position is the equilibrium point, in m?
solution: Set $U'(x) = kx - mg = 0$, giving $x_0 = mg/k$. Numerically $x_0 = (0.75)(9.8)/60 = 0.1225$ m.

name: Value of the centrifugal barrier
statement: A 0.50 kg puck slides on a frictionless table, tethered by a string through a central hole, with angular momentum 2.4 kg m$^2$/s about the hole. The centrifugal term of the effective potential is $L^2/2mr^2$. What is its value at $r = 0.60$ m, in J?
solution: Substituting directly, $L^2/(2mr^2) = (2.4)^2/[2(0.50)(0.60)^2] = 5.76/0.36 = 16.0$ J. This is the rotational kinetic energy $\tfrac12 m r^2\dot\theta^2$ rewritten in terms of $L$.

name: Stable point of a quartic potential
statement: A particle moves in the potential $U(x) = 5x^4 - 20x^2$ ($U$ in J, $x$ in m). What is the positive value of $x$ at which the particle sits in stable equilibrium? Give the answer in m.
solution: $U'(x) = 20x^3 - 40x = 20x(x^2-2)$ vanishes at $x = 0$ and $x = \pm\sqrt2$. Since $U''(x) = 60x^2-40$ is positive at $x = \sqrt2$, that point is stable: $x = 1.414$ m.

name: Period from a measured curvature
statement: A 0.45 kg block rests at a minimum of a complicated potential whose second derivative there is $U''(x_0) = 180$ N/m. What is the period of its small oscillations, in s?
solution: Any smooth minimum behaves like a spring of stiffness $U''(x_0)$, so $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/U''}$. Here $T = 2\pi\sqrt{0.45/180} = 0.3142$ s.

name: Which root is stable
statement: A particle moves in $U(x) = 2x^3 - 9x^2 + 12x$ ($U$ in J, $x$ in m). The potential has two equilibrium points. At which one is the particle stable? Give that value of $x$ in m.
solution: $U'(x) = 6x^2-18x+12 = 6(x-1)(x-2)$, so the equilibria are $x = 1$ m and $x = 2$ m. Since $U''(x) = 12x-18$ is $-6$ at $x=1$ and $+6$ at $x=2$, the stable point is $x = 2.0$ m.

name: Oscillating in that well
statement: A 0.50 kg particle sits at the stable equilibrium of $U(x) = 2x^3-9x^2+12x$ ($U$ in J, $x$ in m) and is nudged slightly. What is the angular frequency of the resulting small oscillations, in rad/s?
solution: The stable point is $x_0 = 2$ m, where $U''(x_0) = 12(2)-18 = 6$ N/m. Then $\omega = \sqrt{U''/m} = \sqrt{6/0.50} = 3.464$ rad/s.

name: Equilibrium of an inverse-power potential
statement: An ion near a surface has $U(x) = \dfrac{4.0}{x^2} - \dfrac{8.0}{x}$, with $U$ in joules when $x$ is in metres. At what value of $x$ does the ion sit in equilibrium? Give the answer in m.

name: Frequency in the inverse-power well
statement: A 0.20 kg particle sits at the minimum of $U(x) = 4.0x^{-2} - 8.0x^{-1}$ (SI units, $x$ in m). What is the angular frequency of its small oscillations about that point, in rad/s?

name: Bead on a rotating hoop
statement: A bead slides without friction on a circular hoop of radius 0.30 m that spins about its vertical diameter at $\Omega = 8.0$ rad/s. Take $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$. At what angle from the downward vertical does the bead settle? Give the answer in degrees.
solution: In the rotating frame $U_{\rm eff}(\theta) = -mgR\cos\theta - \tfrac12 m\Omega^2R^2\sin^2\theta$. Setting $dU_{\rm eff}/d\theta = 0$ off-axis gives $\cos\theta_0 = g/(\Omega^2R) = 9.8/(64\times0.30) = 0.5104$, so $\theta_0 = 59.31^\circ$.

name: Wobble of the bead on the hoop
statement: For the same bead on the hoop of radius 0.30 m spinning at 8.0 rad/s, what is the angular frequency of small oscillations about its off-axis equilibrium, in rad/s?
solution: Differentiating $U_{\rm eff}$ twice at $\theta_0$ gives $mR^2\Omega^2(1-\cos^2\theta_0)$, so $\omega = \Omega\sin\theta_0$. With $\cos\theta_0 = 0.5104$, $\sin\theta_0 = 0.8599$ and $\omega = 6.879$ rad/s.

name: Critical spin of a rotating rod
statement: A 0.30 kg bead slides on a horizontal rod that rotates about a vertical axis through one end; a spring of stiffness 120 N/m connects the bead to the axis. In the rotating frame the effective potential is $\tfrac12(k - m\Omega^2)x^2$. Above what spin rate does the bead fly outward instead of oscillating? Give the answer in rad/s.
solution: The bead is stable only while $k - m\Omega^2 > 0$. The threshold is $\Omega_c = \sqrt{k/m} = \sqrt{120/0.30} = 20.0$ rad/s; above it the effective stiffness is negative and $x = 0$ becomes a maximum.

name: Vibration of a Morse oscillator
statement: A diatomic molecule has the Morse potential $U(r) = D\left[1-e^{-a(r-r_0)}\right]^2$ with $D = 7.0\times10^{-19}$ J and $a = 2.0\times10^{10}$ m$^{-1}$. The vibrating reduced mass is $1.6\times10^{-26}$ kg. What is the angular frequency of small vibrations, in rad/s?
solution: Expanding about $r_0$ gives $U \approx Da^2(r-r_0)^2$, so $U'' = 2Da^2$ and $\omega = a\sqrt{2D/\mu}$. Numerically $\omega = 2.0\times10^{10}\sqrt{1.4\times10^{-18}/1.6\times10^{-26}} = 1.871\times10^{14}$ rad/s.

name: Vibration of an argon pair
statement: Two argon atoms bound by $U(r) = 4\varepsilon[(\sigma/r)^{12}-(\sigma/r)^{6}]$ have $\varepsilon = 1.65\times10^{-21}$ J and $\sigma = 0.340$ nm; the reduced mass of the pair is $3.32\times10^{-26}$ kg. What is the angular frequency of small vibrations about the equilibrium separation, in rad/s?
solution: Differentiating twice and setting $r = 2^{1/6}\sigma$ gives $U''(r_0) = 72\varepsilon/(2^{1/3}\sigma^2) = 57.15\,\varepsilon/\sigma^2 = 0.8156$ N/m. Then $\omega = \sqrt{U''/\mu} = 4.957\times10^{12}$ rad/s.

name: Circular orbit from the angular momentum
statement: For a satellite in Earth orbit the effective potential per unit mass is $U_{\rm eff}(r) = \ell^2/2r^2 - GM/r$, with $GM = 3.986\times10^{14}$ m$^3$/s$^2$. A satellite has specific angular momentum $\ell = 5.30\times10^{10}$ m$^2$/s. What is the radius of its circular orbit, in m?
solution: A circular orbit sits at the minimum of $U_{\rm eff}$: $-\ell^2/r^3 + GM/r^2 = 0$, so $r = \ell^2/GM$. Numerically $r = 2.809\times10^{21}/3.986\times10^{14} = 7.047\times10^{6}$ m.

name: Double-well oscillation
statement: A 0.020 kg slider moves in the double-well potential $U(x) = b(x^2-a^2)^2$ with $b = 500$ J/m$^4$ and $a = 0.10$ m. What is the angular frequency of small oscillations about either minimum, in rad/s?
solution: The minima are at $x = \pm a$, where $U'' = 8ba^2 = 8(500)(0.010) = 40$ N/m. Then $\omega = \sqrt{40/0.020} = 44.72$ rad/s.

name: Charged bead between two fixed charges
statement: Two fixed charges of $+2.0\ \mu$C sit at $x = \pm 0.10$ m. A bead of mass 1.0 g carrying $+2.0\ \mu$C is threaded on the $x$-axis between them. Take $k_e = 8.99\times10^{9}$ N m$^2$/C$^2$. What is the angular frequency of its small oscillations along the axis, in rad/s?
solution: With $U(x) = k_eQq[(d-x)^{-1}+(d+x)^{-1}]$, the second derivative at $x = 0$ is $4k_eQq/d^3 = 143.8$ N/m. Then $\omega = \sqrt{143.8/0.0010} = 379.3$ rad/s.

name: Closest approach in an elliptical orbit
statement: A spacecraft moves in Earth's field with specific energy $E = -1.42\times10^{7}$ J/kg and specific angular momentum $\ell = 6.47\times10^{10}$ m$^2$/s, so $E = \ell^2/2r^2 - GM/r$ at a turning point. Take $GM = 3.986\times10^{14}$ m$^3$/s$^2$. What is its distance of closest approach, in m?
solution: Turning points are the roots of $Er^2 + GMr - \ell^2/2 = 0$. Solving, $r = \left[-GM \pm \sqrt{(GM)^2 + 2E\ell^2}\right]/(2E)$ gives two positive roots; the smaller is the pericentre, $r_{\min} = 6.993\times10^{6}$ m.

name: Apsidal angle for a non-Newtonian force
statement: A particle orbits in the central potential $U(r) = -k/r^{3/2}$ on a nearly circular orbit. For $U = -k/r^{n}$ the radial oscillation frequency satisfies $\omega_r/\omega_\theta = \sqrt{2-n}$. What is the angle swept between successive closest approaches, in rad?
solution: The apsidal angle is $\pi\,\omega_\theta/\omega_r = \pi/\sqrt{2-n}$. With $n = 3/2$, $\sqrt{2-n} = 0.7071$ and the angle is $\pi/0.7071 = 4.443$ rad, larger than $2\pi/2$, so the orbit precesses forward.

name: Radial-to-angular frequency ratio
statement: A particle moves on a nearly circular orbit in the central potential $U(r) = \tfrac12 kr^2$ (a particle tied to the origin by an ideal spring). What is the ratio of its radial oscillation frequency to its orbital angular frequency? Give a pure number.
solution: With $U_{\rm eff} = \ell^2/2r^2 + \tfrac12 kr^2$, the minimum is at $r_0^4 = \ell^2/k$ and $U_{\rm eff}'' = 3\ell^2/r_0^4 + k = 4k$. Since $\omega_\theta^2 = \ell^2/r_0^4 = k$, the ratio is $\sqrt{4k/k} = 2$, which is why the orbit is a closed ellipse centred on the origin.

name: Where the Lennard-Jones force peaks
statement: For $U(r) = 4\varepsilon[(\sigma/r)^{12}-(\sigma/r)^{6}]$ with $\sigma = 0.340$ nm, the attractive force between the atoms has a maximum magnitude at some separation. At what separation does that occur, in nm?
solution: The force is $F = -dU/dr$; its extremum needs $d^2U/dr^2 = 0$, i.e. $156\sigma^{12}/r^{14} = 42\sigma^{6}/r^{8}$. That gives $r = (26/7)^{1/6}\sigma = 1.244(0.340) = 0.4231$ nm, the point beyond which the bond yields.

name: Spinning parabolic wire
statement: A bead slides on a frictionless wire shaped as $y = cx^2$ with $c = 1.5$ m$^{-1}$, and the wire is spun about its vertical symmetry axis at $\Omega = 4.0$ rad/s. Take $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$ and assume $x$ stays small. What is the angular frequency of the bead's small oscillations in the rotating frame, in rad/s?
solution: The effective potential is $U_{\rm eff} = mgcx^2 - \tfrac12 m\Omega^2 x^2$, giving $\omega = \sqrt{2gc - \Omega^2}$. With $2gc = 29.4$ s$^{-2}$ and $\Omega^2 = 16$ s$^{-2}$, $\omega = 3.661$ rad/s; at $\Omega = \sqrt{2gc}$ the bottom goes neutrally stable.

name: Ball rolling in a bowl
statement: A uniform solid ball of radius 2.0 cm rolls without slipping near the bottom of a spherical bowl of radius 20.0 cm. Take $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$. What is the angular frequency of its small oscillations, in rad/s?
solution: The ball's centre moves on a circle of radius $R-r$, and rolling adds rotational inertia so the kinetic energy is $\tfrac{7}{10}m v^2$. Balancing against $U = mg(R-r)\theta^2/2$ gives $\omega = \sqrt{5g/[7(R-r)]} = 6.236$ rad/s.

name: Anharmonic frequency shift
statement: A 0.20 kg mass moves in $U(x) = \tfrac12 kx^2 + \beta x^4$ with $k = 50$ N/m and $\beta = 4.0\times10^{3}$ J/m$^4$, oscillating with amplitude 3.0 cm. To first order in the quartic term the frequency is $\omega \approx \omega_0\left(1 + \tfrac{3\beta A^2}{2k}\right)$. What is the oscillation frequency, in rad/s?
solution: The harmonic frequency is $\omega_0 = \sqrt{50/0.20} = 15.81$ rad/s. The stiffening correction is $3\beta A^2/2k = 3(4000)(9.0\times10^{-4})/100 = 0.108$, so $\omega = 15.81(1.108) = 17.52$ rad/s.

name: Tuning the hoop
statement: A bead slides on a hoop of radius 0.25 m spinning about its vertical diameter at rate $\Omega$. Its off-axis equilibrium sits at $\cos\theta_0 = g/(\Omega^2R)$ and small oscillations about it have frequency $\Omega\sin\theta_0$. Take $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$. At what spin rate is the small-oscillation frequency exactly half the spin rate? Give the answer in rad/s.
solution: The condition $\Omega\sin\theta_0 = \Omega/2$ fixes $\sin\theta_0 = 1/2$, hence $\cos\theta_0 = \sqrt3/2$. Then $\Omega^2 = g/(R\cos\theta_0) = 2g/(\sqrt3 R)$, giving $\Omega = \sqrt{19.6/0.4330} = 6.728$ rad/s.

name: Gauge pressure at the bottom of a pool
statement: A swimming pool is $12.0\,$m deep. Take $\rho_{\text{water}}=1000\,$kg/m$^3$ and $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$. What is the gauge pressure of the water at the bottom, in Pa?
solution: Gauge pressure grows linearly with depth: $p=\rho g h$. Here $p=(1000)(9.8)(12.0)=1.176\times10^5\,$Pa.

name: Absolute pressure on a diver
statement: A diver hangs at a depth of $25.0\,$m in fresh water. Atmospheric pressure is $1.01\times10^5\,$Pa, $\rho_{\text{water}}=1000\,$kg/m$^3$, $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$. What is the absolute pressure on the diver, in Pa?
solution: Absolute pressure is atmospheric plus the water column: $p=p_0+\rho g h$. So $p=1.01\times10^5+(1000)(9.8)(25.0)=3.46\times10^5\,$Pa.

name: Buoyant force on a submerged rock
statement: A rock of volume $3.00\times10^{-3}\,$m$^3$ is completely submerged in water ($\rho=1000\,$kg/m$^3$, $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$). What is the buoyant force on it, in N?
solution: Archimedes' principle: the buoyant force equals the weight of displaced water, $F_B=\rho_{w} g V$. Thus $F_B=(1000)(9.8)(3.00\times10^{-3})=29.4\,$N.

name: Fraction of a pine block underwater
statement: A solid pine block of density $700\,$kg/m$^3$ floats in water ($1000\,$kg/m$^3$). What fraction of the block's volume is below the waterline? Answer as a dimensionless fraction.
solution: Floating means weight equals buoyant force: $\rho_b V g=\rho_w V_{\text{sub}} g$. Therefore $V_{\text{sub}}/V=\rho_b/\rho_w=700/1000=0.700$.

name: Apparent weight of a submerged aluminum block
statement: A $2.50\,$kg aluminum block (density $2700\,$kg/m$^3$) hangs from a spring scale and is fully submerged in water. With $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$ and $\rho_w=1000\,$kg/m$^3$, what does the scale read, in N?
solution: The scale reads true weight minus buoyancy. The block's volume is $2.50/2700=9.259\times10^{-4}\,$m$^3$, so $F_B=(1000)(9.8)(9.259\times10^{-4})=9.07\,$N and the reading is $24.5-9.07=15.43\,$N.

name: Hydraulic car lift
statement: A hydraulic lift has an input piston of area $2.00\times10^{-3}\,$m$^2$ and an output piston of area $5.00\times10^{-2}\,$m$^2$ at the same height. A force of $150\,$N is applied to the input piston. What force does the output piston deliver, in N?
solution: Pascal's principle makes the pressure equal on both pistons, so $F_2=F_1 A_2/A_1$. Here $F_2=150\times(0.0500/0.00200)=3750\,$N.

name: Depth of one atmosphere of water
statement: How deep must you go in fresh water for the gauge pressure to equal one atmosphere, $1.01\times10^5\,$Pa? Use $\rho_w=1000\,$kg/m$^3$ and $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$. Answer in m.
solution: Set $\rho g h=p_0$, so $h=p_0/(\rho g)$. That gives $h=1.01\times10^5/(1000\times9.8)=10.31\,$m.

name: Iceberg in seawater
statement: Ice has density $917\,$kg/m$^3$ and seawater $1025\,$kg/m$^3$. What fraction of a floating iceberg's volume lies below the surface? Answer as a dimensionless fraction.
solution: For a floating body the submerged fraction is the density ratio, $V_{\text{sub}}/V=\rho_{\text{ice}}/\rho_{\text{sea}}$. So the fraction is $917/1025=0.8946$.

name: Height of a mercury barometer
statement: A mercury barometer stands in air at $1.01\times10^5\,$Pa. Mercury has density $13600\,$kg/m$^3$ and $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$. How tall is the mercury column, in m?
solution: The column's weight per unit area balances atmospheric pressure: $\rho g h=p_0$. Hence $h=1.01\times10^5/(13600\times9.8)=0.7576\,$m.

name: Buoyant force of air on a weather balloon
statement: A weather balloon displaces $5.00\,$m$^3$ of air of density $1.225\,$kg/m$^3$. With $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$, what is the buoyant force the air exerts on it, in N?
solution: Air buoyancy obeys the same rule as water: $F_B=\rho_{\text{air}} g V$. So $F_B=(1.225)(9.8)(5.00)=60.03\,$N.

name: Load a wooden raft can carry
statement: A raft is a slab of wood of area $2.00\,$m$^2$, thickness $0.200\,$m, and density $600\,$kg/m$^3$, floating in fresh water. What is the largest mass that can be placed on it before water reaches the top surface, in kg?
solution: At the limit the raft is exactly fully submerged, displacing $V=2.00\times0.200=0.400\,$m$^3$. The buoyant load capacity is $(\rho_w-\rho_{\text{wood}})V=(1000-600)(0.400)=160\,$kg.

name: Open-tube water manometer
statement: A gas line is connected to one arm of an open water manometer. The water in the open arm stands $0.340\,$m higher than in the gas arm. With $\rho_w=1000\,$kg/m$^3$ and $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$, what is the gauge pressure of the gas, in Pa?
solution: The gauge pressure equals the hydrostatic head of the level difference: $p=\rho g \Delta h$. So $p=(1000)(9.8)(0.340)=3332\,$Pa.

name: Density from weight in air and in water
statement: A metal sample weighs $40.0\,$N in air and $32.0\,$N when fully submerged in water ($1000\,$kg/m$^3$). What is the density of the metal, in kg/m$^3$?
solution: The apparent weight loss is the buoyant force, $F_B=8.0\,$N, so the displaced volume is $V=F_B/(\rho_w g)$. The density follows from $\rho=W/(gV)=\rho_w W/F_B=1000\times40.0/8.0=5000\,$kg/m$^3$.

name: Block trapped at an oil-water interface
statement: Oil of density $800\,$kg/m$^3$ floats on water. A block of density $900\,$kg/m$^3$ rests at the interface, partly in each fluid. What fraction of the block's volume is in the water? Answer as a dimensionless fraction.
solution: Equilibrium requires the mean density of the displaced fluids to equal the block's density: $f\rho_w+(1-f)\rho_{\text{oil}}=\rho_b$. Solving, $f=(900-800)/(1000-800)=0.500$.

name: Air column in a diving bell
statement: A diving bell is an open-bottomed cylinder $2.50\,$m tall, initially full of air at $1.01\times10^5\,$Pa. It is lowered until its closed top is $20.0\,$m below the surface. The air stays at constant temperature. Water rises inside until the trapped air column has length $L$, measured down from the closed top. Find $L$, in m. Use $\rho_w=1000\,$kg/m$^3$, $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$.
solution: The trapped air pressure equals the water pressure at the inside water surface, which sits at depth $20.0+L$: $p=p_0+\rho g(20.0+L)$. Boyle's law gives $p_0(2.50)=\big[p_0+\rho g(20.0+L)\big]L$, a quadratic whose positive root is $L=0.8276\,$m.

name: Payload of a hot-air balloon
statement: A hot-air balloon envelope holds $2200\,$m$^3$ of heated air of density $0.950\,$kg/m$^3$; the surrounding air has density $1.225\,$kg/m$^3$. Ignoring the mass of the fabric, what total payload mass can the balloon just lift, in kg?
solution: Lift is the difference between displaced-air weight and the heated air's weight: $m_{\max}=(\rho_{\text{out}}-\rho_{\text{in}})V$. Thus $m_{\max}=(1.225-0.950)(2200)=605\,$kg.

name: Water displaced by a floating ice cube
statement: A $0.200\,$kg ice cube floats in a glass of fresh water ($1000\,$kg/m$^3$). What volume of water does it displace, in m$^3$?
solution: A floating body displaces its own mass of fluid, so $V_{\text{disp}}=m/\rho_w$. That is $0.200/1000=2.00\times10^{-4}\,$m$^3$.

name: Pressure under a layer of oil
statement: A tank holds $0.500\,$m of water with $0.300\,$m of oil (density $850\,$kg/m$^3$) floating on top. With $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$, what is the gauge pressure at the bottom of the tank, in Pa?
solution: Hydrostatic heads add layer by layer: $p=\rho_{\text{oil}} g h_{\text{oil}}+\rho_w g h_w$. So $p=(850)(9.8)(0.300)+(1000)(9.8)(0.500)=2499+4900=7399\,$Pa.

name: Force on a dam face
statement: A vertical dam is $8.00\,$m wide and holds fresh water $4.00\,$m deep against its face, with air on the other side. Using $\rho_w=1000\,$kg/m$^3$ and $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$, what is the net horizontal force from the water on the dam, in N?
solution: Pressure rises linearly with depth, so its average over the wetted face is $\tfrac12\rho g h$. The net force is $F=\tfrac12\rho g h^2 w=\tfrac12(1000)(9.8)(4.00)^2(8.00)=6.272\times10^5\,$N.

name: Volume of a helium balloon that just lifts a load
statement: A helium balloon (helium density $0.166\,$kg/m$^3$) must lift a $2.00\,$kg instrument package plus a $0.300\,$kg envelope in air of density $1.225\,$kg/m$^3$. What is the minimum helium volume, in m$^3$?
solution: Neutral buoyancy requires $(\rho_{\text{air}}-\rho_{\text{He}})V=m_{\text{load}}$. With $m_{\text{load}}=2.30\,$kg, $V=2.30/(1.225-0.166)=2.172\,$m$^3$.

name: Ballast for a neutrally buoyant submarine
statement: A submarine of fixed external volume $250\,$m$^3$ has a hull-and-contents mass of $2.40\times10^5\,$kg. Seawater has density $1025\,$kg/m$^3$. How much seawater must it take into its ballast tanks to hover neutrally submerged, in kg?
solution: Neutral buoyancy means total mass equals displaced seawater mass, $\rho_{\text{sea}}V=1025\times250=2.5625\times10^5\,$kg. The ballast needed is $2.5625\times10^5-2.40\times10^5=1.625\times10^4\,$kg.

name: Extra force to push a float down
statement: A floating cylindrical buoy has cross-sectional area $1.00\times10^{-2}\,$m$^2$ and vertical sides. How much additional downward force is needed to push it $3.00\,$cm deeper into fresh water, in N? Use $\rho_w=1000\,$kg/m$^3$, $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$.
solution: Pushing down by $x$ displaces an extra volume $Ax$, adding buoyancy $\rho_w g A x$. So $F=(1000)(9.8)(0.0100)(0.0300)=2.94\,$N.

name: Bobbing period of a floating cylinder
statement: A wooden cylinder of density $600\,$kg/m$^3$ and height $0.150\,$m floats upright in water with its axis vertical. It is pushed down slightly and released. What is the period of the resulting small vertical oscillation, in s? Use $\rho_w=1000\,$kg/m$^3$, $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$.
solution: A displacement $x$ from equilibrium produces a restoring force $-\rho_w g A x$, so the motion is simple harmonic with $k=\rho_w g A$ and $m=\rho_b A H$. The area cancels: $T=2\pi\sqrt{\rho_b H/(\rho_w g)}=2\pi\sqrt{(600)(0.150)/(1000\times9.8)}=0.6021\,$s.

name: Scale reading with a block hung in the water
statement: A beaker of water sits on a scale; beaker plus water have mass $3.00\,$kg. A metal block of volume $2.50\times10^{-3}\,$m$^3$ hangs from a string and is fully submerged without touching the beaker. What does the scale now read, in N? Use $\rho_w=1000\,$kg/m$^3$, $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$.
solution: By Newton's third law the water pushes up on the block with $F_B$ and the block pushes down on the water with the same $F_B=(1000)(9.8)(2.50\times10^{-3})=24.5\,$N. The scale reads $3.00(9.8)+24.5=53.9\,$N.

name: Depth where a bubble is one third its surface size
statement: A small air bubble released from the bottom of a lake triples in volume by the time it reaches the surface, its temperature staying constant. Using $p_0=1.01\times10^5\,$Pa, $\rho_w=1000\,$kg/m$^3$, $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$, how deep is the lake, in m?
solution: Boyle's law gives $p_d V=p_0(3V)$, so the pressure at depth is $3p_0$. Then $p_0+\rho g d=3p_0$ gives $d=2p_0/(\rho g)=2(1.01\times10^5)/(9800)=20.61\,$m.

name: Oil poured into one arm of a U-tube
statement: A U-tube contains water. A $0.250\,$m column of oil (density $800\,$kg/m$^3$) is poured into the left arm and floats on the water there. By how much does the water level in the right arm stand above the oil-water interface in the left arm, in m?
solution: Match pressures at the oil-water interface level: the oil column there balances an equal-pressure water column in the right arm, $\rho_{\text{oil}} g h_{\text{oil}}=\rho_w g h_w$. So $h_w=0.250(800/1000)=0.200\,$m.

name: How high a released float leaps
statement: A ball of density $300\,$kg/m$^3$ is held $1.20\,$m below the surface of a still pool and released. Neglect drag and the water's inertia. How high above the water surface does its center rise, in m? Use $\rho_w=1000\,$kg/m$^3$, $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$.
solution: While submerged the net upward acceleration is $a=g(\rho_w/\rho_b-1)=9.8(1000/300-1)=22.87\,$m/s$^2$. It leaves the water with $v^2=2a(1.20)=54.88\,$m$^2$/s$^2$, then rises $v^2/(2g)=2.800\,$m.

name: Hydrometer stem reading in a lighter liquid
statement: A hydrometer of total mass $0.0150\,$kg has a uniform stem of cross-sectional area $4.00\times10^{-5}\,$m$^2$. It is floated first in water ($1000\,$kg/m$^3$) and then in a liquid of density $900\,$kg/m$^3$. How much farther down the stem does it sink in the lighter liquid, in m?
solution: Floating requires the same displaced mass in both liquids: $V=m/\rho$. The extra submerged volume is $A\,\Delta h=m(1/\rho_2-1/\rho_1)$, so $\Delta h=(0.0150/4.00\times10^{-5})(1/900-1/1000)=0.0417\,$m.

name: Hinged rod floating at an angle
statement: A uniform rod of length $1.00\,$m and density $500\,$kg/m$^3$ is hinged at one end to the bottom of a tank; the water is $0.600\,$m deep. The rod floats up and rests at an angle $\theta$ above the horizontal, with its lower part submerged. Find $\theta$, in degrees. Use $\rho_w=1000\,$kg/m$^3$.
solution: Take torques about the hinge. The submerged length is $h/\sin\theta$ with its buoyancy acting at half that distance, while the rod's weight acts at $L/2$: $\rho_b L\cdot\tfrac{L}{2}=\rho_w\tfrac{h}{\sin\theta}\cdot\tfrac{h}{2\sin\theta}$. Hence $\sin\theta=\dfrac{h}{L}\sqrt{\rho_w/\rho_b}=0.600\sqrt{2}=0.8485$, giving $\theta=58.05^\circ$.

name: Inner radius of a half-submerged steel shell
statement: A hollow steel sphere (steel density $7800\,$kg/m$^3$) has outer radius $0.200\,$m and a concentric spherical cavity. It floats in water exactly half submerged. What is the inner radius of the cavity, in m? Use $\rho_w=1000\,$kg/m$^3$.
solution: Half submerged means the displaced volume is $\tfrac23\pi R^3$, so $\rho_s\tfrac43\pi(R^3-r^3)=\rho_w\tfrac23\pi R^3$. This gives $r^3=R^3\left(1-\dfrac{\rho_w}{2\rho_s}\right)=R^3(1-0.06410)$, so $r=0.200(0.9359)^{1/3}=0.1956\,$m.

name: Pendulum accelerometer in a train
statement: A small bob hangs from the ceiling of a train car that accelerates forward at $2.50\,$m/s$^2$ on level track. With $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$, what angle does the string make with the vertical, in degrees?
solution: In the car's frame a pseudo-force $ma$ points backward and gravity $mg$ points down; the string lines up with their resultant. Then $\tan\theta=a/g=2.50/9.8$, so $\theta=14.31^\circ$.

name: Tilt of fuel in an accelerating tanker
statement: A tanker truck carries liquid fuel in a partly filled tank and accelerates forward at $3.00\,$m/s$^2$. With $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$, what angle does the free surface of the fuel make with the horizontal, in degrees?
solution: The free surface is always perpendicular to the effective gravity $\vec g_{\text{eff}}=\vec g-\vec a$. Its tilt satisfies $\tan\theta=a/g=3.00/9.8$, giving $\theta=17.01^\circ$.

name: Scale reading in an accelerating elevator
statement: A $70.0\,$kg person stands on a bathroom scale in an elevator accelerating upward at $2.00\,$m/s$^2$. With $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$, what does the scale read, in N?
solution: In the elevator frame the pseudo-force points downward, so the effective gravity is $g+a$. The scale reads $N=m(g+a)=70.0(11.8)=826\,$N.

name: Centrifugal acceleration on a turntable
statement: A small object sits $0.500\,$m from the axis of a turntable spinning at $6.00\,$rad/s. In the rotating frame, what is the magnitude of the centrifugal acceleration it experiences, in m/s$^2$?
solution: The centrifugal acceleration in a rotating frame is $\omega^2 r$ directed outward. Here $\omega^2 r=(6.00)^2(0.500)=18.0\,$m/s$^2$.

name: Minimum speed at the top of a vertical loop
statement: A bucket of water is swung in a vertical circle of radius $1.00\,$m. What is the minimum speed at the top for the water not to fall out, in m/s? Use $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$.
solution: At the minimum speed the bucket exerts no force and gravity alone supplies the centripetal acceleration: $g=v^2/r$. So $v=\sqrt{gr}=\sqrt{9.8}=3.130\,$m/s.

name: Angular speed of a conical pendulum
statement: A conical pendulum has a string of length $1.20\,$m sweeping a cone of half-angle $30.0^\circ$ from the vertical. With $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$, what is its angular speed, in rad/s?
solution: Vertical balance gives $T\cos\theta=mg$ and horizontal gives $T\sin\theta=m\omega^2 L\sin\theta$. Dividing, $\omega=\sqrt{g/(L\cos\theta)}=\sqrt{9.8/(1.20\cos30^\circ)}=3.0708\,$rad/s.

name: Sideways force on a passenger in a curve
statement: A car takes a flat curve of radius $80.0\,$m at a constant $20.0\,$m/s. In the car's frame, what is the magnitude of the centrifugal force felt by a $60.0\,$kg passenger, in N?
solution: The centrifugal force in the car frame is $mv^2/r$. That is $60.0(20.0)^2/80.0=300\,$N.

name: Fastest spin before a coin slides
statement: A coin rests $0.120\,$m from the center of a horizontal turntable; the coefficient of static friction is $0.350$. With $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$, what is the largest angular speed at which the coin stays put, in rad/s?
solution: Friction must supply the centripetal force: $\mu m g \ge m\omega^2 r$. So $\omega_{\max}=\sqrt{\mu g/r}=\sqrt{0.350(9.8)/0.120}=5.3463\,$rad/s.

name: Effective gravity in an accelerating cabin
statement: A sealed cabin accelerates horizontally at $4.00\,$m/s$^2$. With $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$, what is the magnitude of the effective gravitational field inside, in m/s$^2$?
solution: The effective field is the vector sum of $g$ downward and the pseudo-acceleration $a$ horizontally, which are perpendicular. So $g_{\text{eff}}=\sqrt{9.8^2+4.00^2}=10.58\,$m/s$^2$.

name: Apparent weight in a descending elevator
statement: A $5.00\,$kg box rests on the floor of an elevator accelerating downward at $3.00\,$m/s$^2$. With $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$, what normal force does the floor exert, in N?
solution: The effective gravity is reduced to $g-a$. Thus $N=m(g-a)=5.00(6.80)=34.0\,$N.

name: Height difference across an accelerating tank
statement: An open rectangular tank $1.20\,$m long is partly filled with water and accelerated horizontally along its length at $2.00\,$m/s$^2$. With $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$, what is the height difference between the water at the two ends, in m?
solution: The surface tilts with slope $a/g$, so across a length $L$ the rise is $\Delta h=La/g$. Here $\Delta h=1.20(2.00)/9.8=0.2449\,$m.

name: Wedge acceleration that holds a block in place
statement: A block rests on the frictionless $25.0^\circ$ face of a wedge. The wedge is pushed horizontally so the block does not slide relative to it. What is the required acceleration, in m/s$^2$? Use $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$.
solution: In the wedge frame the block must be in equilibrium under gravity, the normal force, and the pseudo-force $ma$. Balancing along the incline gives $ma\cos\theta=mg\sin\theta$, so $a=g\tan25^\circ=4.570\,$m/s$^2$.

name: Rise of the rotating water surface
statement: A cylinder of water rotates about its vertical axis at $8.00\,$rad/s. How much higher is the surface at radius $0.100\,$m than at the axis, in m? Use $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$.
solution: In the rotating frame the free surface is a paraboloid, $z=\omega^2r^2/(2g)$. So $z=(8.00)^2(0.100)^2/(2\times9.8)=0.03265\,$m.

name: Design speed of a banked curve
statement: A highway curve of radius $120\,$m is banked at $12.0^\circ$. At what speed can a car round it with no friction needed, in m/s? Use $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$.
solution: With no friction the normal force alone must tilt to provide the centripetal force: $\tan\theta=v^2/(rg)$. So $v=\sqrt{gr\tan\theta}=\sqrt{9.8(120)\tan12^\circ}=15.8103\,$m/s.

name: Pressure at the back of an accelerating tank
statement: An open tank $1.00\,$m long holds water whose depth would be $0.400\,$m at rest. The tank accelerates horizontally at $3.00\,$m/s$^2$ along its length. What is the gauge pressure at the bottom of the rear wall, in Pa? Use $\rho_w=1000\,$kg/m$^3$, $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$.
solution: The surface tilts with slope $a/g$ about the tank's midpoint, so the rear depth becomes $h_0+La/(2g)=0.400+0.1531=0.5531\,$m. The pressure there is still $\rho g h$ measured vertically: $p=(1000)(9.8)(0.5531)=5420.0\,$Pa.

name: Acceleration that pins a crate to a wall
statement: A crate is pressed against the vertical inside back wall of a truck by the wall itself as the truck accelerates forward. The coefficient of static friction between crate and wall is $0.400$. What minimum forward acceleration keeps the crate from sliding down, in m/s$^2$? Use $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$.
solution: The wall's normal force is $N=ma$, and friction must hold the weight: $\mu ma\ge mg$. So $a_{\min}=g/\mu=9.8/0.400=24.5\,$m/s$^2$.

name: Pendulum period in an accelerating cart
statement: A simple pendulum of length $0.800\,$m hangs inside a cart accelerating horizontally at $5.00\,$m/s$^2$. What is the period of small oscillations about its tilted equilibrium, in s? Use $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$.
solution: Small oscillations use the effective gravity $g_{\text{eff}}=\sqrt{g^2+a^2}=\sqrt{9.8^2+5.00^2}=11.00\,$m/s$^2$. Then $T=2\pi\sqrt{L/g_{\text{eff}}}=2\pi\sqrt{0.800/11.00}=1.6943\,$s.

name: Spin rate for artificial gravity
statement: A ring-shaped space station of radius $90.0\,$m spins to give its rim an effective gravity of $9.8\,$m/s$^2$. What is the required angular speed, in rad/s?
solution: The centrifugal acceleration at the rim must equal $g$: $\omega^2 R=g$. So $\omega=\sqrt{9.8/90.0}=0.3300\,$rad/s.

name: Acceleration inside a laboratory centrifuge
statement: A centrifuge spins a sample at radius $0.0800\,$m at $4000\,$rev/min. What is the magnitude of the centrifugal acceleration in the rotating frame, in m/s$^2$?

name: Coriolis acceleration of a polar aircraft
statement: An aircraft flies horizontally at $200\,$m/s directly over the North Pole. Earth's angular speed is $7.292\times10^{-5}\,$rad/s. What is the magnitude of the Coriolis acceleration in Earth's rotating frame, in m/s$^2$?
solution: The Coriolis acceleration is $2\vec\Omega\times\vec v$; at the pole the velocity is perpendicular to $\vec\Omega$, so the magnitude is $2\Omega v$. That gives $2(7.292\times10^{-5})(200)=0.02917\,$m/s$^2$.

name: Effective gravity at the equator
statement: Ignoring Earth's oblateness, take the true gravitational field to be $9.8\,$m/s$^2$, Earth's radius $6.371\times10^6\,$m, and $\Omega=7.292\times10^{-5}\,$rad/s. What is the effective free-fall acceleration measured at the equator, in m/s$^2$?
solution: At the equator the centrifugal acceleration points straight up and subtracts: $g_{\text{eff}}=g-\Omega^2R$. With $\Omega^2R=(7.292\times10^{-5})^2(6.371\times10^6)=0.03387$, $g_{\text{eff}}=9.7661\,$m/s$^2$.

name: Hanging air freshener in a turning car
statement: A small ornament hangs from the mirror of a car driving at a steady $12.0\,$m/s around a flat circular track of radius $25.0\,$m. What angle does its string make with the vertical, in degrees? Use $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$.
solution: In the car's rotating frame the bob hangs along the resultant of gravity and the outward centrifugal force $mv^2/r$. Thus $\tan\theta=v^2/(rg)=144/(25.0\times9.8)$, so $\theta=30.45^\circ$.

name: Spin that uncovers the bottom of a bucket
statement: A cylindrical bucket of radius $0.150\,$m holds water $0.200\,$m deep and is spun about its vertical axis. The bucket is tall enough that nothing spills. At what angular speed does the paraboloid surface just touch the center of the bottom, in rad/s? Use $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$.
solution: Volume conservation puts the vertex a distance $\omega^2R^2/(4g)$ below the original level and the rim the same distance above. Setting $\omega^2R^2/(4g)=0.200$ gives $\omega=\sqrt{4(9.8)(0.200)/(0.150)^2}=18.6667\,$rad/s.

name: Minimum push on a wedge with friction
statement: A block sits on the $30.0^\circ$ face of a wedge; the coefficient of static friction is $0.250$. The wedge is accelerated horizontally toward the incline so the block does not slide down. What is the minimum acceleration, in m/s$^2$? Use $g=9.8\,$m/s$^2$.
solution: Work in the wedge frame with friction at its maximum acting up the slope. Along and normal to the incline, $ma\cos\theta+\mu N=mg\sin\theta$ with $N=mg\cos\theta+ma\sin\theta$, giving $a=g\dfrac{\tan\theta-\mu}{1+\mu\tan\theta}=2.8034\,$m/s$^2$.

name: Pressure difference in a full accelerating tank
statement: A sealed tank $2.00\,$m long is completely filled with water and accelerated horizontally at $4.00\,$m/s$^2$ along its length. What is the pressure difference between the rear and front walls at the same height, in Pa? Use $\rho_w=1000\,$kg/m$^3$.
solution: In the accelerating frame the pseudo-force per unit volume $\rho a$ acts backward, so pressure grows linearly toward the rear: $dp/dx=-\rho a$. Over $L=2.00\,$m, $\Delta p=\rho a L=(1000)(4.00)(2.00)=8000\,$Pa.
