statement: A vacuum gap in a high-voltage feedthrough carries a field of $1.5\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{V/m}$. What is the electrostatic energy density, in $\mathrm{J/m^3}$?
solution: Use $u=\tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2$. So $u=\tfrac12(8.85\times10^{-12})(1.5\times10^{6})^2=9.956\,\mathrm{J/m^3}$.

name: Breakdown voltage of a film
statement: A polypropylene film $0.15\,\mathrm{mm}$ thick has a dielectric strength of $16\,\mathrm{MV/m}$. What is the largest voltage the film can hold off, in V?
solution: Breakdown occurs when the uniform field $E=V/d$ reaches the dielectric strength, so $V_{\max}=E_{\max}d$. Thus $V_{\max}=(1.6\times10^{7})(1.5\times10^{-4})=2400\,\mathrm{V}$.

name: Energy in a ceramic capacitor
statement: A ceramic capacitor of $22.0\,\mathrm{nF}$ is charged to $150\,\mathrm{V}$. How much energy does it store, in $\mu$J?

name: Charge on a water-filled cell
statement: A capacitance cell measures $35.0\,\mathrm{pF}$ when empty. It is filled with pure water ($\kappa=80.0$) and connected to a $12.0\,\mathrm{V}$ source. What charge sits on its plates, in nC?
solution: The filled capacitance is $\kappa C_0=(80.0)(35.0\,\mathrm{pF})=2.80\,\mathrm{nF}$, and $Q=CV$. So $Q=(2.80\times10^{-9})(12.0)=3.360\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{C}=33.60\,\mathrm{nC}$.

name: Bound surface charge density
statement: A dielectric slab with $\kappa=5.0$ fills the gap of a capacitor whose plates carry free surface charge density $4.0\,\mu\mathrm{C/m^2}$. What is the magnitude of the bound surface charge density on the slab face, in $\mu\mathrm{C/m^2}$?
solution: The net density producing the field inside is $\sigma_f/\kappa$, so the bound density is $\sigma_b=\sigma_f(1-1/\kappa)$. Thus $\sigma_b=4.0(1-0.20)=3.20\,\mu\mathrm{C/m^2}$, opposite in sign to the adjacent plate.

name: On-chip oxide capacitor
statement: An on-chip capacitor uses a $2.0\,\mathrm{mm}\times2.0\,\mathrm{mm}$ electrode over a silicon-dioxide layer $0.50\,\mu\mathrm{m}$ thick, with $\kappa=3.9$. What is its capacitance, in pF?
solution: Use $C=\kappa\varepsilon_0A/d$ with $A=4.0\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m^2}$. Then $C=(3.9)(8.85\times10^{-12})(4.0\times10^{-6})/(5.0\times10^{-7})=2.761\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{F}=276.1\,\mathrm{pF}$.

name: Energy density inside a dielectric
statement: Inside a polyethylene insulator ($\kappa=2.2$) the electric field is $5.0\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{V/m}$. What is the energy density, in $\mathrm{J/m^3}$?
solution: In a linear dielectric $u=\tfrac12\kappa\varepsilon_0E^2$. So $u=\tfrac12(2.2)(8.85\times10^{-12})(5.0\times10^{6})^2=243.4\,\mathrm{J/m^3}$.

name: Partially filling slab
statement: A parallel-plate capacitor has plate area $0.010\,\mathrm{m^2}$ and a $1.00\,\mathrm{mm}$ gap. A slab of thickness $0.60\,\mathrm{mm}$ with $\kappa=4.0$ is inserted parallel to the plates, leaving air elsewhere. What is the capacitance, in pF?
solution: The slab and the remaining air act as two capacitors in series, giving $C=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d-t+t/\kappa}$. The effective gap is $1.00-0.60+0.15=0.55\,\mathrm{mm}$, so $C=(8.85\times10^{-12})(0.010)/(5.5\times10^{-4})=1.609\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{F}=160.9\,\mathrm{pF}$.

name: Half-area dielectric
statement: A capacitor with plate area $0.010\,\mathrm{m^2}$ and gap $1.00\,\mathrm{mm}$ has a slab of $\kappa=6.0$ that fills the gap completely but covers only half the plate area. What is the capacitance, in pF?
solution: The two halves share the same voltage, so they are capacitors in parallel: $C=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0(A/2)}{d}(1+\kappa)$. Numerically $C=(8.85\times10^{-12})(0.005)(7.0)/(1.0\times10^{-3})=3.098\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{F}=309.8\,\mathrm{pF}$.

name: Two stacked dielectric layers
statement: A capacitor of plate area $0.010\,\mathrm{m^2}$ has its gap filled by two stacked layers: $0.40\,\mathrm{mm}$ of $\kappa=2.0$ material and $0.60\,\mathrm{mm}$ of $\kappa=5.0$ material. What is the capacitance, in pF?
solution: Stacked layers carry the same free charge, so they are in series: $1/C=d_1/(\kappa_1\varepsilon_0A)+d_2/(\kappa_2\varepsilon_0A)$. This gives an effective gap $0.40/2.0+0.60/5.0=0.32\,\mathrm{mm}$, so $C=(8.85\times10^{-12})(0.010)/(3.2\times10^{-4})=276.6\,\mathrm{pF}$.

name: Removing a slab at constant charge
statement: A capacitor with $C_0=100\,\mathrm{pF}$ empty is filled with a slab of $\kappa=3.0$ and charged to $50.0\,\mathrm{V}$, then disconnected. How much work must be done to pull the slab all the way out, in nJ?
solution: Disconnected means $Q$ is fixed at $Q=\kappa C_0V=1.50\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{C}$, and $U=Q^2/(2C)$ rises as $C$ drops from $\kappa C_0$ to $C_0$. So $W=\dfrac{Q^2}{2C_0}\left(1-\dfrac1\kappa\right)=\dfrac{(1.5\times10^{-8})^2}{2(10^{-10})}(0.6667)=750.0\,\mathrm{nJ}$.

name: Inserting a slab at constant voltage
statement: An empty capacitor $C_0=100\,\mathrm{pF}$ stays connected to a $50.0\,\mathrm{V}$ battery while a slab with $\kappa=3.0$ is slid in to fill it completely. How much work does the battery do, in nJ?
solution: The extra charge delivered is $\Delta Q=(\kappa-1)C_0V$, and the battery does $W_{\rm batt}=V\Delta Q=(\kappa-1)C_0V^2$. So $W_{\rm batt}=(2)(10^{-10})(2500)=5.00\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{J}=500.0\,\mathrm{nJ}$; half of it becomes stored field energy and half is delivered to whatever pulls the slab in.

name: Total bound charge on a face
statement: A slab with $\kappa=5.0$ fills a capacitor of plate area $0.020\,\mathrm{m^2}$ whose free surface charge density is $4.0\,\mu\mathrm{C/m^2}$. What is the magnitude of the total bound charge on one face of the slab, in nC?
solution: The bound density is $\sigma_b=\sigma_f(1-1/\kappa)=3.20\,\mu\mathrm{C/m^2}$, and the total is $\sigma_bA$. So $Q_b=(3.20\times10^{-6})(0.020)=6.40\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{C}=64.00\,\mathrm{nC}$.

name: Maximum energy before breakdown
statement: A capacitor uses a $0.10\,\mathrm{mm}$ layer of a dielectric with $\kappa=2.6$ and strength $25\,\mathrm{MV/m}$, over plates of area $0.050\,\mathrm{m^2}$. What is the maximum energy it can store, in mJ?
solution: The maximum energy density is $u=\tfrac12\kappa\varepsilon_0E_{\max}^2=7191\,\mathrm{J/m^3}$, and the dielectric volume is $Ad=5.0\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m^3}$. So $U=uAd=0.03595\,\mathrm{J}=35.95\,\mathrm{mJ}$.

name: Extra charge drawn from the battery
statement: A $47\,\mathrm{pF}$ air capacitor is held at $9.0\,\mathrm{V}$ by a battery while a slab of $\kappa=5.5$ is inserted to fill it. How much additional charge flows onto the plates, in pC?
solution: At fixed $V$ the charge is $Q=CV$, so $\Delta Q=(\kappa-1)C_0V$. Thus $\Delta Q=(4.5)(47\times10^{-12})(9.0)=1.904\times10^{-9}\,\mathrm{C}=1904\,\mathrm{pC}$.

name: Polyethylene coaxial cable
statement: A coaxial cable has an inner conductor of radius $1.2\,\mathrm{mm}$, an outer shield of inner radius $4.0\,\mathrm{mm}$, and polyethylene ($\kappa=2.3$) between them. What is the capacitance per unit length, in pF/m?
solution: For a coaxial line, $C/L=2\pi\kappa\varepsilon_0/\ln(b/a)$. With $\ln(4.0/1.2)=1.204$, $C/L=2\pi(2.3)(8.85\times10^{-12})/1.204=1.062\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{F/m}=106.2\,\mathrm{pF/m}$.

name: Field in the air gap beside a slab
statement: A $1.00\,\mathrm{mm}$ gap held at $200\,\mathrm{V}$ contains a $0.60\,\mathrm{mm}$ slab of $\kappa=4.0$ lying flat against one plate, with air filling the rest. What is the field in the air region, in V/m?
solution: $D$ is the same in both regions, so $E_{\rm slab}=E_{\rm air}/\kappa$, and $V=E_{\rm air}(d-t)+ (E_{\rm air}/\kappa)t$. Solving, $E_{\rm air}=V/(d-t+t/\kappa)=200/(5.5\times10^{-4})=3.636\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{V/m}$.

name: Effective dielectric constant of a half-filled gap
statement: A slab of $\kappa=6.0$ fills exactly half the thickness of a parallel-plate gap, with vacuum in the other half. By what factor is the capacitance increased over the empty value (dimensionless)?
solution: The two halves are in series: $\dfrac{1}{C}=\dfrac{d/2}{\kappa\varepsilon_0A}+\dfrac{d/2}{\varepsilon_0A}$, so $C/C_0=\dfrac{2\kappa}{1+\kappa}$. With $\kappa=6.0$ the factor is $12/7=1.714$ — far less than $\kappa$, because the vacuum half dominates the series.

name: Energy in a filled capacitor
statement: A capacitor with plate area $0.008\,\mathrm{m^2}$ and a $0.30\,\mathrm{mm}$ gap is filled with a dielectric of $\kappa=2.5$ and charged to $60.0\,\mathrm{V}$. How much energy is stored, in $\mu$J?

name: Force pulling a slab into a live capacitor
statement: A parallel-plate capacitor is held at $500\,\mathrm{V}$ by a battery. Its plates are $8.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ wide with a $0.50\,\mathrm{mm}$ gap, and a slab with $\kappa=4.0$ is partly inserted. What is the magnitude of the force pulling the slab further in, in mN?
solution: At constant $V$ the force is $F=\tfrac12V^2\,dC/dx$ with $C(x)=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0w}{d}[L+(\kappa-1)x]$, so $F=\dfrac{(\kappa-1)\varepsilon_0wV^2}{2d}$ — independent of how far the slab is in. Numerically $F=(3)(8.85\times10^{-12})(0.080)(2.5\times10^{5})/(10^{-3})=5.310\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{N}=0.5310\,\mathrm{mN}$.

name: Force on a slab at fixed charge
statement: A capacitor has square plates $10.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ long and $6.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ wide with a $0.40\,\mathrm{mm}$ gap, and carries a fixed charge of $20.0\,\mathrm{nC}$ (battery disconnected). A slab with $\kappa=3.0$ is inserted a distance $5.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ along the plates. What is the magnitude of the force pulling it in, in mN?
solution: At fixed charge $U=Q^2/2C$ and $F=-dU/dx=\dfrac{Q^2}{2C^2}\dfrac{dC}{dx}$, with $\dfrac{dC}{dx}=\dfrac{(\kappa-1)\varepsilon_0w}{d}$. Here $C=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0w}{d}[L+(\kappa-1)x]=2.655\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{F}$ and $dC/dx=2.655\times10^{-9}\,\mathrm{F/m}$, giving $F=(4.0\times10^{-16})(2.655\times10^{-9})/[2(7.049\times10^{-20})]=7.533\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{N}=0.007533\,\mathrm{mN}$.

name: Which layer breaks down first
statement: A cable insulation stack has $0.20\,\mathrm{mm}$ of material A ($\kappa=3.0$, strength $20\,\mathrm{MV/m}$) on top of $0.30\,\mathrm{mm}$ of material B ($\kappa=6.0$, strength $10\,\mathrm{MV/m}$). What is the maximum voltage across the stack before either layer breaks down, in V?
solution: $D=\kappa\varepsilon_0E$ is common to both layers, so the allowed $D$ is $\min(\kappa_1\varepsilon_0E_1,\kappa_2\varepsilon_0E_2)$: A allows $D=5.31\times10^{-4}$ and B allows $D=5.31\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{C/m^2}$ — they fail simultaneously. Then $V=E_1t_1+E_2t_2=(2.0\times10^{7})(2.0\times10^{-4})+(1.0\times10^{7})(3.0\times10^{-4})=7000\,\mathrm{V}$.

name: Fraction of energy in the vacuum half
statement: A parallel-plate capacitor at fixed charge has its gap half-filled (by thickness) with a slab of $\kappa=4.0$, vacuum in the other half. What fraction of the total stored energy sits inside the dielectric (dimensionless)?
solution: $D$ is the same everywhere, so $E_{\rm diel}=E_{\rm vac}/\kappa$ and $u=\tfrac12\kappa\varepsilon_0E^2$ gives $u_{\rm diel}/u_{\rm vac}=1/\kappa$. Equal volumes then put a fraction $\dfrac{1/\kappa}{1+1/\kappa}=\dfrac{1}{\kappa+1}=0.2000$ of the energy in the slab.

name: Hemispherically filled spherical capacitor
statement: A spherical capacitor with inner radius $5.00\,\mathrm{cm}$ and outer radius $7.00\,\mathrm{cm}$ has its lower hemisphere filled with oil ($\kappa=2.2$) and its upper hemisphere left empty. What is the capacitance, in pF?
solution: Both hemispheres see the same potential difference, so they are capacitors in parallel, each with half the full-shell capacitance $4\pi\varepsilon_0ab/(b-a)$. Hence $C=2\pi\varepsilon_0(1+\kappa)\dfrac{ab}{b-a}=2\pi(8.85\times10^{-12})(3.2)(0.175)=3.114\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{F}=31.14\,\mathrm{pF}$.

name: Kinetic energy gained by a slab
statement: An empty capacitor of $250\,\mathrm{pF}$ is held at $120\,\mathrm{V}$ by a battery. A frictionless slab with $\kappa=2.8$ is released at the edge and slides in until it fills the gap. What is its kinetic energy at that moment, in nJ?
solution: The battery supplies $W_{\rm batt}=V\Delta Q=(\kappa-1)C_0V^2$ while the stored energy rises by $\Delta U=\tfrac12(\kappa-1)C_0V^2$. The difference goes to the slab: $KE=\tfrac12(\kappa-1)C_0V^2=\tfrac12(1.8)(2.5\times10^{-10})(14400)=3.240\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{J}=3240\,\mathrm{nJ}$.

name: Graded dielectric
statement: A capacitor with plate area $0.020\,\mathrm{m^2}$ and gap $2.00\,\mathrm{mm}$ is filled with a material whose dielectric constant varies linearly from $\kappa=2.0$ at one plate to $\kappa=6.0$ at the other. What is the capacitance, in pF?
solution: Treat the gap as infinitely many thin series capacitors: $\dfrac1C=\int_0^d\dfrac{dx}{\kappa(x)\varepsilon_0A}$ with $\kappa(x)=\kappa_1+(\kappa_2-\kappa_1)x/d$. The integral gives $C=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0A(\kappa_2-\kappa_1)}{d\ln(\kappa_2/\kappa_1)}$, so $C=(8.85\times10^{-12})(0.020)(4.0)/[(2.0\times10^{-3})(1.0986)]=3.222\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{F}=322.2\,\mathrm{pF}$.

name: Dielectric liquid rising between plates
statement: Two vertical parallel plates separated by $0.50\,\mathrm{mm}$ dip into a reservoir of water ($\kappa=80.0$, density $1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$) and are held at $300\,\mathrm{V}$. Ignoring surface tension and taking $g=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, how high does the water rise between the plates, in mm?
solution: The electrical force per unit width pulling liquid up is $\dfrac{(\kappa-1)\varepsilon_0V^2}{2d}$, balanced by the weight of the raised column $\rho g h d$ per unit width. Solving, $h=\dfrac{(\kappa-1)\varepsilon_0V^2}{2\rho g d^2}$; with the numbers $h=(79)(8.85\times10^{-12})(9.0\times10^{4})/[2(1000)(9.81)(2.5\times10^{-7})]=0.01283\,\mathrm{m}=12.83\,\mathrm{mm}$.

name: Charge through a toaster
statement: A toaster element carries a steady current of $8.5\ \mathrm{A}$ while the toaster runs for $90\ \mathrm{s}$. How much charge passes through the element, in $\mathrm{C}$?
solution: Steady current means $Q=It$. So $Q=(8.5\ \mathrm{A})(90\ \mathrm{s})=765\ \mathrm{C}$.

name: Electrons into a phone
statement: A phone charger delivers a steady $2.0\ \mathrm{A}$ to the phone for exactly one hour. How many electrons flow through the charging cable? Use $e=1.6\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$. Give a pure number.
solution: The charge delivered is $Q=It=(2.0)(3600)=7200\ \mathrm{C}$. Dividing by the electron charge, $N=Q/e=7200/(1.6\times10^{-19})=4.5\times10^{22}$.

name: Resistance of an extension cord
statement: An extension cord uses copper wire of diameter $1.63\ \mathrm{mm}$ and resistivity $\rho=1.68\times10^{-8}\ \Omega\cdot\mathrm{m}$. The cord is $15\ \mathrm{m}$ long, so the current travels $30\ \mathrm{m}$ (out along one conductor and back along the other). What is the total resistance of the cord, in $\Omega$?

name: Headlight current
statement: A car headlight bulb has a hot resistance of $2.4\ \Omega$ and is connected across a $12.0\ \mathrm{V}$ source. What current does it draw, in $\mathrm{A}$?
solution: Ohm's law gives $I=V/R=12.0/2.4=5.0\ \mathrm{A}$.

name: Three resistors in series
statement: Resistors of $4.0\ \Omega$, $6.0\ \Omega$ and $10.0\ \Omega$ are wired end to end in a single loop with an ideal $12.0\ \mathrm{V}$ battery. What is the current in the loop, in $\mathrm{A}$?
solution: Series resistances add: $R=4.0+6.0+10.0=20.0\ \Omega$. Then $I=V/R=12.0/20.0=0.60\ \mathrm{A}$.

name: Two heaters in parallel
statement: A $60\ \Omega$ heating coil and a $30\ \Omega$ heating coil are connected in parallel between the same two terminals. What is the resistance of the combination, in $\Omega$?
solution: For parallel resistors $1/R=1/60+1/30=1/20$, so $R=20\ \Omega$. The combination is always smaller than the smaller resistor.

name: Hair dryer power
statement: A hair dryer draws $12.5\ \mathrm{A}$ from a $120\ \mathrm{V}$ outlet. What electrical power does it consume, in $\mathrm{W}$?
solution: Power delivered to a device is $P=IV=(12.5)(120)=1500\ \mathrm{W}$.

name: Heat in a cable
statement: A welding cable of resistance $8.0\ \Omega$ carries $3.0\ \mathrm{A}$. At what rate is energy dissipated as heat in the cable, in $\mathrm{W}$?
solution: Use $P=I^{2}R$ because the current is what is given: $P=(3.0)^{2}(8.0)=72\ \mathrm{W}$.

name: Resistance of a toaster element
statement: A toaster is rated $1200\ \mathrm{W}$ when connected to $120\ \mathrm{V}$. What is the resistance of its heating element at operating temperature, in $\Omega$?
solution: With voltage and power known, $P=V^{2}/R$, so $R=V^{2}/P=(120)^{2}/1200=12\ \Omega$.

name: A cell with internal resistance
statement: A AA cell of emf $1.50\ \mathrm{V}$ and internal resistance $0.30\ \Omega$ is connected to a $2.70\ \Omega$ lamp. What current flows, in $\mathrm{A}$?
solution: The internal resistance is in series with the load, so $I=\mathcal{E}/(R+r)=1.50/(2.70+0.30)=0.50\ \mathrm{A}$.

name: Drift speed in a lamp cord
statement: A copper lamp cord of diameter $2.05\ \mathrm{mm}$ carries $5.0\ \mathrm{A}$. Copper has $n=8.5\times10^{28}$ free electrons per cubic meter and $e=1.6\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$. What is the drift speed of the electrons, in $\mathrm{m/s}$?
solution: The current is $I=nAev_d$, so $v_d=I/(nAe)$. Here $A=\pi d^{2}/4=3.301\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m^2}$, giving $v_d=5.0/[(8.5\times10^{28})(3.301\times10^{-6})(1.6\times10^{-19})]=1.11\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Electrons crawl even though the signal is fast.

name: Hot tungsten filament
statement: A tungsten lamp filament has resistance $0.30\ \Omega$ at $20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Tungsten has temperature coefficient $\alpha=4.5\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}$ referred to $20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Estimate the filament resistance when it runs at $2400^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, in $\Omega$.
solution: Use the linear model $R=R_0[1+\alpha(T-T_0)]$. With $\Delta T=2380\ \mathrm{K}$, $R=0.30[1+(4.5\times10^{-3})(2380)]=0.30(11.71)=3.51\ \Omega$. This is why a cold bulb draws a large inrush current.

name: Stretching a wire
statement: A wire of resistance $2.0\ \Omega$ is drawn through a die until its length is three times the original. The volume of metal and the resistivity are unchanged. What is the new resistance, in $\Omega$?
solution: Constant volume means $A$ falls by the same factor the length grows, so $R=\rho L/A\propto L^{2}$. Tripling the length multiplies the resistance by $9$: $R=9(2.0)=18\ \Omega$.

name: A series-parallel network
statement: Starting at one battery terminal, a $4.0\ \Omega$ resistor leads to node A. From A, a $6.0\ \Omega$ resistor and a $12.0\ \Omega$ resistor run in parallel to node B. From B a $2.0\ \Omega$ resistor returns to the other terminal. What is the resistance between the battery terminals, in $\Omega$?
solution: The parallel pair gives $(6)(12)/(6+12)=4.0\ \Omega$. That is in series with the other two, so $R=4.0+4.0+2.0=10.0\ \Omega$.

name: Finding internal resistance
statement: A battery of emf $12.00\ \mathrm{V}$ shows a terminal voltage of $11.40\ \mathrm{V}$ while delivering $3.00\ \mathrm{A}$ to a load. What is its internal resistance, in $\Omega$?
solution: The terminal voltage is $V=\mathcal{E}-Ir$, so $r=(\mathcal{E}-V)/I=(12.00-11.40)/3.00=0.200\ \Omega$.

name: A voltmeter that loads the circuit
statement: Two $10.0\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$ resistors are in series across an ideal $24.0\ \mathrm{V}$ supply. A voltmeter of internal resistance $10.0\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$ is connected across the lower resistor. What voltage does the meter read, in $\mathrm{V}$?
solution: The meter is in parallel with the lower resistor, giving $5.0\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$. The divider now reads $V=24.0\times5.0/(10.0+5.0)=8.00\ \mathrm{V}$, not the $12.0\ \mathrm{V}$ present before the meter was attached.

name: Ammeter burden
statement: A $6.00\ \mathrm{V}$ ideal source drives a $4.00\ \Omega$ resistor. An ammeter of resistance $0.500\ \Omega$ is inserted in series to measure the current. By how much is the ammeter reading below the current that flowed before the meter was inserted, in $\mathrm{A}$?
solution: Before insertion $I=6.00/4.00=1.500\ \mathrm{A}$; afterwards $I=6.00/4.50=1.333\ \mathrm{A}$. The reading is low by $0.167\ \mathrm{A}$, about $11\%$.

name: Maximum power from a battery
statement: A $9.00\ \mathrm{V}$ battery has internal resistance $1.20\ \Omega$. A variable resistor is connected across it and adjusted for maximum power delivered to that resistor. What is that maximum power, in $\mathrm{W}$?
solution: Power in the load is $P=\mathcal{E}^{2}R/(R+r)^{2}$, which is maximized at $R=r$. Then $P_{\max}=\mathcal{E}^{2}/(4r)=81.0/4.80=16.9\ \mathrm{W}$; half the chemical power is wasted inside the battery.

name: Cutting a nichrome heater
statement: A heater is to be wound from nichrome wire of diameter $0.400\ \mathrm{mm}$ and resistivity $1.10\times10^{-6}\ \Omega\cdot\mathrm{m}$, and must have resistance $24.0\ \Omega$. What length of wire is needed, in $\mathrm{m}$?
solution: From $R=\rho L/A$, $L=RA/\rho$. The cross section is $A=\pi(4.00\times10^{-4})^{2}/4=1.257\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m^2}$, so $L=(24.0)(1.257\times10^{-7})/(1.10\times10^{-6})=2.74\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Two loads on one battery
statement: A $12.0\ \mathrm{V}$ ideal car battery feeds two devices in parallel: a fan of resistance $8.00\ \Omega$ and a radio of resistance $24.0\ \Omega$. What total power does the battery deliver, in $\mathrm{W}$?
solution: Each branch sees the full $12.0\ \mathrm{V}$, so $P=V^{2}/R$ for each: $144/8.00=18.0\ \mathrm{W}$ and $144/24.0=6.00\ \mathrm{W}$. The total is $24.0\ \mathrm{W}$.

name: Two bulbs in series
statement: Two bulbs are rated $60.0\ \mathrm{W}$ and $100\ \mathrm{W}$ at $120\ \mathrm{V}$. Treat each as a fixed resistor equal to its rated value. The two are wired in series across a $120\ \mathrm{V}$ line. What power does the $60.0\ \mathrm{W}$ bulb now dissipate, in $\mathrm{W}$?
solution: The rated resistances are $R_{60}=120^{2}/60.0=240\ \Omega$ and $R_{100}=144\ \Omega$. In series $I=120/384=0.3125\ \mathrm{A}$, so $P_{60}=I^{2}R_{60}=(0.3125)^{2}(240)=23.4\ \mathrm{W}$. In series the larger resistance (the lower-wattage bulb) glows brighter.

name: Current density in house wiring
statement: A household branch circuit uses copper wire of diameter $2.59\ \mathrm{mm}$ and carries $15.0\ \mathrm{A}$. What is the magnitude of the current density in the wire, in $\mathrm{A/m^2}$?
solution: Current density is $J=I/A$ with $A=\pi d^{2}/4=\pi(2.59\times10^{-3})^{2}/4=5.269\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m^2}$. Then $J=15.0/5.269\times10^{-6}=2.85\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{A/m^2}$.

name: Half a wire stretched
statement: A uniform wire has resistance $3.00\ \Omega$. Exactly half of its length is stretched until that half is twice as long as it was, at constant volume; the other half is untouched. What is the resistance of the whole wire now, in $\Omega$?
solution: Each half starts at $1.50\ \Omega$. Stretching at constant volume gives $R\propto L^{2}$, so the stretched half becomes $4(1.50)=6.00\ \Omega$ while the other stays $1.50\ \Omega$. In series the total is $7.50\ \Omega$.

name: A tapered contact pin
statement: A copper contact pin is a truncated cone of length $20.0\ \mathrm{mm}$ whose circular cross section has radius $1.00\ \mathrm{mm}$ at one end and $3.00\ \mathrm{mm}$ at the other, with the radius varying linearly. Current flows along the axis and the current density may be taken as uniform over each cross section. With $\rho=1.68\times10^{-8}\ \Omega\cdot\mathrm{m}$, what is the end-to-end resistance, in $\Omega$?
solution: Add thin slices in series: $R=\int_0^{L}\rho\,dx/[\pi r(x)^{2}]$ with $r$ linear in $x$. The integral evaluates to $R=\rho L/(\pi ab)$, the geometric-mean-area result. Numerically $R=(1.68\times10^{-8})(0.0200)/[\pi(1.00\times10^{-3})(3.00\times10^{-3})]=3.565\times10^{-5}\ \Omega$.

name: Operating temperature of a filament
statement: A $100\ \mathrm{W}$, $120\ \mathrm{V}$ incandescent bulb has a cold filament resistance of $4.50\ \Omega$ measured at $20.0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Tungsten has $\alpha=4.5\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}$ referred to $20.0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, and the linear model is assumed valid. Estimate the operating temperature of the filament, in $^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.
solution: The hot resistance follows from the rating: $R_{hot}=V^{2}/P=120^{2}/100=144\ \Omega$. Then $R_{hot}/R_{cold}=1+\alpha\Delta T$ gives $\Delta T=(144/4.50-1)/(4.5\times10^{-3})=6.889\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{K}$, so $T\approx6.91\times10^{3}\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The linear model badly overestimates; real filaments run near $2800\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.

name: Best load at the end of a long cable
statement: A generator of emf $24.0\ \mathrm{V}$ and internal resistance $0.500\ \Omega$ feeds a load through a cable whose total resistance is $1.50\ \Omega$. The load resistance can be chosen freely. What is the greatest power that can be delivered to the load, in $\mathrm{W}$?
solution: Everything in series with the load acts as one source resistance $r_{\rm eff}=0.500+1.50=2.00\ \Omega$, and the load power peaks when $R=r_{\rm eff}$. Then $P_{\max}=\mathcal{E}^{2}/(4r_{\rm eff})=576/8.00=72.0\ \mathrm{W}$.

name: Correcting for meter resistance
statement: A $30.0\ \mathrm{V}$ ideal supply drives a $20.0\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$ resistor in series with an unknown resistor $R$. A voltmeter of internal resistance $50.0\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$ placed across $R$ reads $10.0\ \mathrm{V}$. What is $R$, in $\Omega$?
solution: With the meter attached, the current through the $20.0\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$ resistor splits between $R$ and the meter. Junction rule: $(30.0-10.0)/20.0\mathrm{k}=10.0/R+10.0/50.0\mathrm{k}$, so $10.0/R=1.00\times10^{-3}-0.200\times10^{-3}$ and $R=1.25\times10^{4}\ \Omega$. Ignoring the meter would have given $10.0\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$.

name: An infinite ladder
statement: An infinite ladder is built from identical cells: from the input node a $2.00\ \Omega$ resistor leads to the next node, a $3.00\ \Omega$ resistor connects that node to the return rail, and the pattern repeats forever. What is the input resistance of the ladder, in $\Omega$?
solution: Self-similarity: adding one more cell must not change the input resistance, so $R=2.00+(3.00R)/(3.00+R)$. This gives $R^{2}-2.00R-6.00=0$, whose positive root is $R=1+\sqrt{7}=3.65\ \Omega$.

name: Resistor cube
statement: Twelve identical $6.00\ \Omega$ resistors are soldered along the twelve edges of a cube. What is the resistance between two diagonally opposite corners of the cube, in $\Omega$?
solution: By symmetry the three edges leaving the input corner carry equal currents $I/3$, the six middle edges carry $I/6$, and the three edges into the far corner carry $I/3$. Summing potential drops along a path gives $V=IR(1/3+1/6+1/3)=5IR/6$, so $R_{eq}=5(6.00)/6=5.00\ \Omega$.

name: Leakage through cable insulation
statement: A coaxial cable $0.500\ \mathrm{m}$ long has an inner conductor of radius $2.00\ \mathrm{mm}$ and an outer conductor of inner radius $5.00\ \mathrm{mm}$. The insulation between them has resistivity $2.00\times10^{5}\ \Omega\cdot\mathrm{m}$. Leakage current flows radially outward from the inner to the outer conductor. What is the leakage resistance between the conductors, in $\Omega$?
solution: Treat the insulation as nested cylindrical shells in series: a shell of radius $r$ and thickness $dr$ has $dR=\rho\,dr/(2\pi rL)$. Integrating, $R=\frac{\rho}{2\pi L}\ln(b/a)=\frac{2.00\times10^{5}}{2\pi(0.500)}\ln(2.50)=5.83\times10^{4}\ \Omega$.

name: Junction in a fuse box
statement: At a junction inside a fuse box, one wire brings in $2.50\ \mathrm{A}$ and two wires carry current away. One of the outgoing wires carries $0.80\ \mathrm{A}$. What current does the other outgoing wire carry, in $\mathrm{A}$?
solution: Charge cannot pile up at a junction, so current in equals current out: $2.50=0.80+I$, giving $I=1.70\ \mathrm{A}$.

name: Batteries in opposition
statement: A $12.0\ \mathrm{V}$ battery and a $9.00\ \mathrm{V}$ battery are wired in a single loop with their positive terminals facing each other, so their emfs oppose. The loop also contains $6.00\ \Omega$ of total resistance. What current flows around the loop, in $\mathrm{A}$?
solution: Going once around, the two emfs subtract: $12.0-9.00-I(6.00)=0$. So $I=3.00/6.00=0.500\ \mathrm{A}$, driven by the stronger battery.

name: Drop across the middle resistor
statement: An ideal $9.00\ \mathrm{V}$ battery drives a single loop containing $10.0\ \Omega$, $20.0\ \Omega$ and $30.0\ \Omega$ in series. What is the potential difference across the $20.0\ \Omega$ resistor, in $\mathrm{V}$?
solution: The loop rule gives one current: $I=9.00/60.0=0.150\ \mathrm{A}$. Then $V=IR=(0.150)(20.0)=3.00\ \mathrm{V}$.

name: Two cells in series
statement: Two $1.50\ \mathrm{V}$ cells, each of internal resistance $0.250\ \Omega$, are connected in series (positive to negative) and drive a $4.50\ \Omega$ bulb. What current flows, in $\mathrm{A}$?
solution: The emfs add and all resistances are in series: $I=(1.50+1.50)/(4.50+0.250+0.250)=3.00/5.00=0.600\ \mathrm{A}$.

name: Charging a battery
statement: A charger forces $5.00\ \mathrm{A}$ backwards through a battery of emf $12.0\ \mathrm{V}$ and internal resistance $0.400\ \Omega$. What is the potential difference across the battery terminals while charging, in $\mathrm{V}$?
solution: When current is pushed into the positive terminal the $Ir$ drop adds instead of subtracting: $V=\mathcal{E}+Ir=12.0+(5.00)(0.400)=14.0\ \mathrm{V}$.

name: A four-wire junction
statement: Four wires meet at a node. Two carry current into the node, $3.00\ \mathrm{A}$ and $1.50\ \mathrm{A}$; a third carries $2.20\ \mathrm{A}$ away. What current does the fourth wire carry away from the node, in $\mathrm{A}$?
solution: The junction rule gives $3.00+1.50=2.20+I$, so $I=2.30\ \mathrm{A}$ out of the node.

name: Unknown emf in a loop
statement: A single loop contains a $15.0\ \mathrm{V}$ battery, an unknown battery connected so that it opposes the first, and $20.0\ \Omega$ of resistance. The measured current is $0.500\ \mathrm{A}$. What is the emf of the unknown battery, in $\mathrm{V}$?
solution: Loop rule: $15.0-\mathcal{E}-I(20.0)=0$ with $I=0.500\ \mathrm{A}$. The resistive drop is $10.0\ \mathrm{V}$, so $\mathcal{E}=5.00\ \mathrm{V}$.

name: Opposing cells with a load
statement: A $6.00\ \mathrm{V}$ cell of internal resistance $1.00\ \Omega$ and a $4.50\ \mathrm{V}$ cell of internal resistance $0.500\ \Omega$ are wired in one loop with a $3.00\ \Omega$ resistor, with the cells opposing each other. What current flows in the loop, in $\mathrm{A}$?
solution: The net emf is $6.00-4.50=1.50\ \mathrm{V}$ and all resistances are in series: $R=1.00+0.500+3.00=4.50\ \Omega$. Hence $I=1.50/4.50=0.333\ \mathrm{A}$.

name: Terminal voltage under load
statement: A $9.00\ \mathrm{V}$ battery with internal resistance $1.00\ \Omega$ delivers $1.50\ \mathrm{A}$ to an external circuit. What is the potential difference between its terminals, in $\mathrm{V}$?
solution: Walking from the negative to the positive terminal inside the battery, $V=\mathcal{E}-Ir=9.00-(1.50)(1.00)=7.50\ \mathrm{V}$.

name: Current into a parallel pair
statement: An ideal $12.0\ \mathrm{V}$ source is connected across a $4.00\ \Omega$ resistor and a $12.0\ \Omega$ resistor that are in parallel with each other. What total current does the source deliver, in $\mathrm{A}$?
solution: Both branches see $12.0\ \mathrm{V}$: $3.00\ \mathrm{A}$ and $1.00\ \mathrm{A}$. The junction rule at the source terminal gives $4.00\ \mathrm{A}$ total.

name: Two batteries feeding one load
statement: Two batteries are connected in parallel across the same load. Battery 1 has emf $12.00\ \mathrm{V}$ and internal resistance $0.200\ \Omega$; battery 2 has emf $12.60\ \mathrm{V}$ and internal resistance $0.300\ \Omega$; their positive terminals are joined at node A and their negative terminals at node B. A $1.50\ \Omega$ load also connects A to B. What current flows through the load, in $\mathrm{A}$?
solution: Let $V$ be the voltage across the load. The junction rule at A gives $(12.00-V)/0.200+(12.60-V)/0.300=V/1.50$. Solving, $V=11.33\ \mathrm{V}$ and the load current is $V/1.50=7.56\ \mathrm{A}$.

name: Alternator charging a battery
statement: A car alternator of emf $14.40\ \mathrm{V}$ and internal resistance $0.100\ \Omega$ is connected through cable of resistance $0.150\ \Omega$ to a battery of emf $12.20\ \mathrm{V}$ and internal resistance $0.0500\ \Omega$, positive to positive. No other load is connected. What charging current flows, in $\mathrm{A}$?
solution: The two emfs oppose, so the loop rule gives $14.40-12.20=I(0.100+0.150+0.0500)$. Hence $I=2.20/0.300=7.33\ \mathrm{A}$ into the battery's positive terminal.

name: Superposition at a shared node
statement: Nodes A and B are joined by three parallel branches: branch 1 is a $12.0\ \mathrm{V}$ battery in series with $2.00\ \Omega$ (positive terminal toward A), branch 2 is a bare $4.00\ \Omega$ resistor, and branch 3 is a $6.00\ \mathrm{V}$ battery in series with $3.00\ \Omega$ (positive terminal toward A). What current flows through the $4.00\ \Omega$ resistor, in $\mathrm{A}$?
solution: Take B as zero and let $V_A$ be unknown. The junction rule at A reads $(12.0-V_A)/2.00+(6.00-V_A)/3.00=V_A/4.00$, so $V_A=7.385\ \mathrm{V}$. The resistor current is $V_A/4.00=1.85\ \mathrm{A}$ from A to B.

name: Thevenin for a loaded divider
statement: An ideal $12.0\ \mathrm{V}$ supply drives a divider: $6.00\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$ from the positive terminal to node A, and $3.00\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$ from A back to the negative terminal. A $2.00\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$ load is then connected between A and the negative terminal. What current flows in the load, in $\mathrm{A}$?
solution: Thevenin: with the load removed, $V_{th}=12.0(3.00/9.00)=4.00\ \mathrm{V}$; killing the source, $R_{th}=6.00\|3.00=2.00\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$. The load current is $4.00/(2.00+2.00)\mathrm{k}=1.00\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{A}$.

name: A battery buried in a branch
statement: A $24.0\ \mathrm{V}$ ideal battery has its positive terminal at node A and its negative terminal at node B. A $4.00\ \Omega$ resistor runs from A to node C. Two branches connect C to B: a bare $6.00\ \Omega$ resistor, and a $12.0\ \Omega$ resistor in series with a $6.00\ \mathrm{V}$ battery whose positive terminal faces C. What current flows through the $4.00\ \Omega$ resistor, in $\mathrm{A}$?
solution: Take $V_B=0$, $V_A=24.0\ \mathrm{V}$. The junction rule at C is $(24.0-V_C)/4.00=V_C/6.00+(V_C-6.00)/12.0$, giving $V_C=13.0\ \mathrm{V}$. Then $I=(24.0-13.0)/4.00=2.75\ \mathrm{A}$.

name: Reading across an unbalanced bridge
statement: A $12.0\ \mathrm{V}$ ideal supply is connected across two parallel divider strings. String 1 is $10.0\ \Omega$ from the positive rail to node A, then $30.0\ \Omega$ from A to the negative rail. String 2 is $20.0\ \Omega$ from the positive rail to node B, then $20.0\ \Omega$ from B to the negative rail. An ideal voltmeter (infinite resistance) is connected between A and B. What is the magnitude of its reading, in $\mathrm{V}$?
solution: An ideal meter draws no current, so each string is an ordinary divider: $V_A=12.0(30.0/40.0)=9.00\ \mathrm{V}$ and $V_B=12.0(20.0/40.0)=6.00\ \mathrm{V}$ above the negative rail. The reading is $|V_A-V_B|=3.00\ \mathrm{V}$; the bridge is not balanced.

name: Power in the shared branch
statement: Node B is grounded. A $9.00\ \mathrm{V}$ battery holds node A at $+9.00\ \mathrm{V}$ relative to B. A $3.00\ \Omega$ resistor joins A to node N. From N, a $6.00\ \Omega$ resistor runs to B, and a second branch from N to B consists of a $2.00\ \Omega$ resistor in series with a $3.00\ \mathrm{V}$ battery whose positive terminal faces N. What power is dissipated in the $6.00\ \Omega$ resistor, in $\mathrm{W}$?

name: Three cells across one lamp
statement: Three batteries are connected in parallel between nodes A and B, all with positive terminals at A: $6.00\ \mathrm{V}$ with $1.00\ \Omega$ internal resistance, $9.00\ \mathrm{V}$ with $2.00\ \Omega$, and $12.0\ \mathrm{V}$ with $3.00\ \Omega$. A $4.00\ \Omega$ lamp also connects A to B. What is the current in the $6.00\ \mathrm{V}$ battery branch, in $\mathrm{A}$? Report a negative value if that battery is being charged.
solution: Let $V$ be the A-to-B voltage. The junction rule gives $\sum(\mathcal{E}_i-V)/r_i=V/4.00$, i.e. $14.5=V(1+0.5+0.333+0.25)$, so $V=6.960\ \mathrm{V}$. The first branch carries $(6.00-6.960)/1.00=-0.960\ \mathrm{A}$: the weakest cell is being charged by the others.

name: A two-rung ladder
statement: An ideal $18.0\ \mathrm{V}$ battery has its positive terminal connected through a $2.00\ \Omega$ resistor to node N. A $4.00\ \Omega$ resistor connects N to the negative rail. Also from N, a $3.00\ \Omega$ resistor leads to node M, and a $6.00\ \Omega$ resistor connects M to the negative rail. What current flows in the $4.00\ \Omega$ resistor, in $\mathrm{A}$?
solution: The $3.00$ and $6.00\ \Omega$ in series give $9.00\ \Omega$, in parallel with $4.00\ \Omega$ gives $2.769\ \Omega$. The battery current is $18.0/4.769=3.774\ \mathrm{A}$, so $V_N=3.774(2.769)=10.45\ \mathrm{V}$ and the $4.00\ \Omega$ carries $10.45/4.00=2.61\ \mathrm{A}$.

name: Who is powering the headlights?
statement: Three branches connect node N to the car chassis (taken as zero potential): an alternator of emf $14.00\ \mathrm{V}$ with internal resistance $0.100\ \Omega$, a battery of emf $12.40\ \mathrm{V}$ with internal resistance $0.0500\ \Omega$, and a headlight load of $1.40\ \Omega$. Both sources have their positive terminals at N. What is the magnitude of the current in the battery branch, in $\mathrm{A}$?
solution: Junction rule at N: $(14.00-V)/0.100+(12.40-V)/0.0500=V/1.40$, giving $V=12.633\ \mathrm{V}$. The battery branch carries $(12.40-12.633)/0.0500=-4.65\ \mathrm{A}$, so $4.65\ \mathrm{A}$ flows into the battery: the alternator runs the lights and charges the battery.

name: Capacitor in a steady circuit
statement: An ideal $9.00\ \mathrm{V}$ battery drives $2.00\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$ in series with $4.00\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$. A branch containing a $1.00\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$ resistor in series with a capacitor is connected across the $4.00\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$ resistor. Long after the switch closes, what is the potential difference across the capacitor, in $\mathrm{V}$?
solution: In the steady state no current flows in the capacitor branch, so the $1.00\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$ resistor has no drop and the capacitor sees the full voltage across the $4.00\ \mathrm{k}\Omega$ resistor. The divider gives $V=9.00(4.00/6.00)=6.00\ \mathrm{V}$.

name: Voltage between two taps
statement: A $15.0\ \mathrm{V}$ ideal battery has its positive terminal at A and its negative terminal at B. Two independent strings connect A to B: string 1 is $5.00\ \Omega$ from A to node P then $10.0\ \Omega$ from P to B; string 2 is $20.0\ \Omega$ from A to node Q then $10.0\ \Omega$ from Q to B. Nothing else connects P and Q. What is $V_P-V_Q$, in $\mathrm{V}$?
solution: Each string is an independent divider referenced to B: $V_P=15.0(10.0/15.0)=10.0\ \mathrm{V}$ and $V_Q=15.0(10.0/30.0)=5.00\ \mathrm{V}$. Hence $V_P-V_Q=5.00\ \mathrm{V}$.

name: Current through the galvanometer
statement: A bridge is built as follows. An ideal $6.00\ \mathrm{V}$ source connects node S (positive) to node G (negative). From S, $100\ \Omega$ goes to node A and $150\ \Omega$ goes to node B. From A, $200\ \Omega$ goes to G; from B, $250\ \Omega$ goes to G. A galvanometer of resistance $50.0\ \Omega$ bridges A to B. What is the magnitude of the current in the galvanometer, in $\mathrm{A}$?
solution: The bridge is unbalanced ($100/200\neq150/250$), so write node equations at A and B with $V_S=6.00\ \mathrm{V}$, $V_G=0$. Solving $ (6-V_A)/100=V_A/200+(V_A-V_B)/50$ and $(6-V_B)/150+(V_A-V_B)/50=V_B/250$ gives $V_A=3.921\ \mathrm{V}$, $V_B=3.861\ \mathrm{V}$, so $I_g=(V_A-V_B)/50.0=1.19\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{A}$ from A to B.

name: Three meshes
statement: Consider three meshes sharing branches. Mesh 1 contains a $20.0\ \mathrm{V}$ battery, a $10.0\ \Omega$ resistor of its own, the $5.00\ \Omega$ resistor shared with mesh 2, and the $4.00\ \Omega$ resistor shared with mesh 3. Mesh 2 contains a $10.0\ \mathrm{V}$ battery opposing its clockwise mesh current, an $8.00\ \Omega$ resistor of its own, the shared $5.00\ \Omega$, and the $6.00\ \Omega$ shared with mesh 3. Mesh 3 contains a $12.0\ \Omega$ resistor of its own plus the shared $4.00\ \Omega$ and $6.00\ \Omega$. All three mesh currents are defined clockwise, and the $20.0\ \mathrm{V}$ battery drives mesh 1 clockwise. What is the mesh current of mesh 1, in $\mathrm{A}$?
solution: Mesh analysis gives $19i_1-5i_2-4i_3=20$, $-5i_1+19i_2-6i_3=-10$, $-4i_1-6i_2+22i_3=0$. Solving the system yields $i_1=1.022\ \mathrm{A}$, $i_2=-0.217\ \mathrm{A}$, $i_3=0.127\ \mathrm{A}$.

name: Thevenin equivalent of a bridge
statement: Take the bridge of the previous type: an ideal $6.00\ \mathrm{V}$ source from S to G, with $100\ \Omega$ from S to A, $200\ \Omega$ from A to G, $150\ \Omega$ from S to B, and $250\ \Omega$ from B to G. Nothing is connected between A and B. Find the Thevenin resistance seen looking into terminals A and B, in $\Omega$.
solution: Kill the ideal source by shorting S to G. Then $100\ \Omega$ and $200\ \Omega$ appear in parallel between A and the shorted rail ($66.67\ \Omega$), and $150\ \Omega$ with $250\ \Omega$ in parallel at B ($93.75\ \Omega$). These are in series between A and B: $R_{th}=160.4\ \Omega$.

name: A bank of unequal batteries
statement: Three batteries are paralleled across a $0.900\ \Omega$ load, all positive terminals at node A and all negative terminals at node B: $12.60\ \mathrm{V}$ with $0.100\ \Omega$, $12.00\ \mathrm{V}$ with $0.150\ \Omega$, and $11.40\ \mathrm{V}$ with $0.200\ \Omega$. What is the current in the $12.00\ \mathrm{V}$ battery, in $\mathrm{A}$? Use a negative value if that battery is being charged.
solution: Let $V$ be the load voltage. The junction rule at A gives $\sum(\mathcal{E}_i-V)/r_i=V/0.900$, i.e. $126+80+57=V(10+6.667+5+1.111)$, so $V=11.546\ \mathrm{V}$. The middle battery then carries $(12.00-11.546)/0.150=3.02\ \mathrm{A}$ (discharging).

name: Deducing a hidden resistor
statement: An ideal $24.0\ \mathrm{V}$ battery drives a $3.00\ \Omega$ resistor from its positive terminal to node N. Two branches run from N back to the negative terminal: a $12.0\ \Omega$ resistor and an unknown resistor $R$. An ammeter shows $1.20\ \mathrm{A}$ in the $12.0\ \Omega$ branch. What is $R$, in $\Omega$?
solution: The known branch fixes the node voltage: $V_N=(1.20)(12.0)=14.4\ \mathrm{V}$. The $3.00\ \Omega$ resistor then carries $(24.0-14.4)/3.00=3.20\ \mathrm{A}$, so the junction rule leaves $3.20-1.20=2.00\ \mathrm{A}$ for $R$, giving $R=14.4/2.00=7.20\ \Omega$.

name: Resistance of an unbalanced bridge
statement: Five resistors form a bridge between terminals S and G: $2.00\ \Omega$ from S to A, $3.00\ \Omega$ from A to G, $4.00\ \Omega$ from S to B, $5.00\ \Omega$ from B to G, and $6.00\ \Omega$ from A to B. What is the resistance between S and G, in $\Omega$?
solution: The bridge is unbalanced ($2/3\neq4/5$), so no series-parallel reduction works; inject $1.00\ \mathrm{A}$ at S with $V_G=0$ and solve the node equations for $V_S$. The result is $V_S=3.212\ \mathrm{V}$, hence $R_{SG}=3.21\ \Omega$.

name: Loaded bridge with a real battery
statement: A battery of emf $9.00\ \mathrm{V}$ and internal resistance $0.500\ \Omega$ has its positive terminal connected to node S and its negative terminal to node G. From S, $4.00\ \Omega$ leads to node A and $8.00\ \Omega$ leads to node B. From A, $6.00\ \Omega$ leads to G; from B, $5.00\ \Omega$ leads to G. A galvanometer of resistance $10.0\ \Omega$ connects A to B. What is the total current delivered by the battery, in $\mathrm{A}$?
solution: Write node equations for $V_S$, $V_A$, $V_B$ with $V_G=0$, including the internal resistance branch $(9.00-V_S)/0.500$. Solving gives $V_S=8.257\ \mathrm{V}$, $V_A=4.679\ \mathrm{V}$, $V_B=3.529\ \mathrm{V}$, and the battery current is $(9.00-V_S)/0.500=1.49\ \mathrm{A}$. Equivalently the bridge presents about $5.56\ \Omega$.

name: Two supplies sharing a bus
statement: A grounded rail is at zero potential. An ideal $20.0\ \mathrm{V}$ supply holds node S1 at $+20.0\ \mathrm{V}$ and an ideal $10.0\ \mathrm{V}$ supply holds node S2 at $+10.0\ \mathrm{V}$, both referenced to the rail. A $5.00\ \Omega$ resistor joins S1 to node A, and a $5.00\ \Omega$ resistor joins S2 to node B. A $10.0\ \Omega$ resistor joins A to B. Each of A and B is also joined to the rail by its own $20.0\ \Omega$ resistor. What current flows from A to B through the $10.0\ \Omega$ resistor, in $\mathrm{A}$?
solution: Two unknown node voltages suffice. At A: $(20.0-V_A)/5.00=V_A/20.0+(V_A-V_B)/10.0$; at B: $(10.0-V_B)/5.00+(V_A-V_B)/10.0=V_B/20.0$. Solving gives $V_A=14.22\ \mathrm{V}$ and $V_B=9.778\ \mathrm{V}$, so $I_{AB}=(14.22-9.778)/10.0=0.444\ \mathrm{A}$ from A to B.

name: Time constant of a simple RC loop
statement: A $4.7\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor is connected in series with an uncharged $100\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor and a battery. Find the time constant $\tau$ of the circuit, in seconds.
solution: The time constant of a single-loop RC circuit is $\tau = RC$. Here $\tau = (4700\ \Omega)(1.00\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{F}) = 0.470\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Half-life of a discharge
statement: A $22\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor is charged and then discharged through a $10\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor. How long does it take for the capacitor voltage to fall to half its initial value, in seconds?
solution: Discharge follows $V = V_0 e^{-t/RC}$, so the half-life is $t_{1/2} = RC\ln 2$. With $RC = 0.220\ \mathrm{s}$, $t_{1/2} = 0.220\times 0.6931 = 0.1525\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Final charge on a capacitor
statement: A $470\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor is connected through a resistor to a $12\ \mathrm{V}$ battery and left for a long time. Find the final charge on the capacitor, in coulombs.
solution: After a long time no current flows, so there is no drop across the resistor and the capacitor sits at the full battery voltage. Then $Q = CV = (4.70\times10^{-4})(12) = 5.64\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{C}$.

name: Initial current into an uncharged capacitor
statement: A $9.0\ \mathrm{V}$ battery, a $3.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor, and an uncharged capacitor are connected in a single loop by closing a switch at $t=0$. Find the current immediately after the switch closes, in amperes.
solution: An uncharged capacitor has zero voltage across it, so at $t=0$ it behaves like a plain wire. The whole battery voltage sits across the resistor: $I_0 = 9.0/3000 = 3.00\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{A}$.

name: Steady-state current with a capacitor branch
statement: A $12\ \mathrm{V}$ battery drives current through a $1.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor to node $A$. From $A$ a $2.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor returns to the battery's negative terminal, and a $100\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor is also connected from $A$ to the negative terminal. Find the battery current a long time after the switch is closed, in amperes.
solution: At $t=\infty$ the capacitor is fully charged and carries no current, so it acts as an open branch. The battery then sees $1.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}+2.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$, giving $I = 12/3000 = 4.00\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{A}$.

name: Energy in a camera flash capacitor
statement: A camera flash stores its energy in a $120\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor charged to $350\ \mathrm{V}$. Find the stored energy, in joules.
solution: The energy stored on a capacitor is $U = \tfrac12 CV^2$. Here $U = \tfrac12 (1.20\times10^{-4})(350)^2 = 7.35\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Voltage left after a fixed time
statement: A $20\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor charged to $100\ \mathrm{V}$ is discharged through a $50\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor starting at $t=0$. Find the capacitor voltage at $t = 2.5\ \mathrm{s}$, in volts.

name: Heat produced while charging
statement: A $470\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor is charged from zero to full through a resistor by a $9.0\ \mathrm{V}$ battery. Find the total energy dissipated as heat in the resistor over the whole charging process, in joules.
solution: The battery delivers $QV = CV^2$ while the capacitor stores only $\tfrac12 CV^2$; the missing half becomes heat, independently of $R$. So $W_R = \tfrac12 CV^2 = \tfrac12(4.70\times10^{-4})(81) = 0.0190\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Time to reach 90 percent charge
statement: A $10\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor charges through a $33\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor from a battery. How long after the switch closes does the charge reach $90\%$ of its final value, in seconds?
solution: Charging gives $Q = Q_f(1-e^{-t/\tau})$, so $0.10 = e^{-t/\tau}$ and $t = \tau\ln 10$. With $\tau = 0.330\ \mathrm{s}$, $t = 0.330\times2.3026 = 0.760\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Two capacitors in series
statement: A $10\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ and a $15\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor are wired in series with each other, and this pair is placed in series with a $100\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor and a battery. Find the time constant of the circuit, in seconds.
solution: Capacitors in series combine as $1/C = 1/C_1 + 1/C_2$, giving $C = (10)(15)/(25) = 6.0\ \mu\mathrm{F}$. Then $\tau = RC = (1.0\times10^5)(6.0\times10^{-6}) = 0.600\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Defibrillator energy delivered in 5 ms
statement: A defibrillator charges a $32\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor to $5000\ \mathrm{V}$ and then discharges it through a patient's chest, modelled as a $50\ \Omega$ resistor. Find the energy delivered to the chest during the first $5.0\ \mathrm{ms}$, in joules.
solution: The capacitor voltage decays with $\tau = RC = 1.60\ \mathrm{ms}$, and the remaining stored energy goes as $e^{-2t/\tau}$. Energy delivered is $\tfrac12 CV_0^2\,(1-e^{-2t/\tau}) = 400\,(1-e^{-6.25}) = 399.2\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Thevenin time constant of a divider
statement: A $12\ \mathrm{V}$ battery feeds node $A$ through a $6.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor. A $3.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor runs from $A$ to ground, and a $100\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor also runs from $A$ to ground. Find the time constant for charging the capacitor, in seconds.
solution: Kill the battery (replace it by a wire) and look back from the capacitor: the two resistors appear in parallel, $R_{th} = (6)(3)/(9) = 2.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$. Then $\tau = R_{th}C = (2000)(1.0\times10^{-4}) = 0.200\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Final capacitor voltage in a divider
statement: A $12\ \mathrm{V}$ battery feeds node $A$ through a $6.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor; a $3.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor runs from $A$ to ground and a $100\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor also runs from $A$ to ground. Find the capacitor voltage after a long time, in volts.
solution: At steady state the capacitor draws no current, so the two resistors form an ordinary divider. $V_A = 12\cdot 3/(6+3) = 4.00\ \mathrm{V}$.

name: Battery current at the instant of closing
statement: A $12\ \mathrm{V}$ battery feeds node $A$ through a $6.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor; a $3.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor runs from $A$ to ground and an uncharged $100\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor also runs from $A$ to ground. Find the battery current immediately after the switch closes, in amperes.
solution: At $t=0$ the uncharged capacitor holds node $A$ at $0\ \mathrm{V}$, shorting out the $3.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor. All the battery current flows through the $6.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor: $I = 12/6000 = 2.00\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{A}$.

name: Charge remaining after three time constants
statement: A capacitor discharges through a resistor. Find the fraction of its original charge that remains after three time constants have elapsed. Answer as a dimensionless number.
solution: The charge obeys $Q = Q_0 e^{-t/\tau}$, so after $t = 3\tau$ the fraction left is $e^{-3} = 0.0498$.

name: Time for the stored energy to halve
statement: A $500\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor discharges through a $100\ \Omega$ resistor. How long does it take for the stored energy to fall to half its initial value, in seconds?
solution: Since $V \propto e^{-t/\tau}$, the energy $\tfrac12 CV^2 \propto e^{-2t/\tau}$, so the energy half-life is half the voltage half-life: $t = (\tau/2)\ln 2$. With $\tau = 0.0500\ \mathrm{s}$, $t = 0.01733\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Parallel capacitors bleeding down
statement: A $4.7\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ and a $2.2\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor are connected in parallel across a $220\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ bleeder resistor. Both start at $50\ \mathrm{V}$. How long does it take the voltage to fall to $5.0\ \mathrm{V}$, in seconds?
solution: Parallel capacitors add: $C = 4.7+2.2 = 6.9\ \mu\mathrm{F}$, so $\tau = (2.20\times10^5)(6.9\times10^{-6}) = 1.518\ \mathrm{s}$. Falling by a factor of $10$ takes $t = \tau\ln 10 = 3.50\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Final charge with a resistor in the capacitor branch
statement: A $24\ \mathrm{V}$ battery feeds node $A$ through a $1.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor. A $2.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor runs from $A$ to ground. A second branch from $A$ to ground consists of a $3.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor in series with a $220\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor. Find the final charge on the capacitor, in coulombs.
solution: At steady state no current flows in the capacitor branch, so the $3.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor drops nothing and the capacitor sits at $V_A$. The divider gives $V_A = 24\cdot 2/(1+2) = 16.0\ \mathrm{V}$, so $Q = (2.20\times10^{-4})(16.0) = 3.52\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{C}$.

name: Time constant with a series branch resistor
statement: A $24\ \mathrm{V}$ battery feeds node $A$ through a $1.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor, a $2.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor runs from $A$ to ground, and a branch from $A$ to ground holds a $3.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor in series with a $220\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor. Find the charging time constant, in seconds.
solution: Short the battery and look back from the capacitor terminals: the $3.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ is in series with the parallel pair $1.0\,\|\,2.0 = 0.667\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$, so $R_{th} = 3667\ \Omega$. Then $\tau = R_{th}C = 0.807\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Dissipated power one time constant in
statement: A capacitor charged to $24\ \mathrm{V}$ discharges through a $1.2\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor. Find the instantaneous power dissipated in the resistor at the moment $t=\tau$, in watts.
solution: The resistor power is $P = V^2/R = (V_0^2/R)e^{-2t/\tau}$. At $t=\tau$ this is $(576/1200)e^{-2} = 0.480\times0.1353 = 0.0650\ \mathrm{W}$.

name: Peak power in a flash tube
statement: A camera flash uses an $800\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor charged to $300\ \mathrm{V}$, which is dumped through a flash tube of resistance $5.0\ \Omega$. Find the peak power delivered to the tube, in watts.
solution: Power peaks at $t=0$, when the full $300\ \mathrm{V}$ still stands across the tube. Then $P = V_0^2/R = 90000/5.0 = 1.80\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{W}$.

name: Settling to one percent
statement: A sample-and-hold circuit has a charging time constant of $2.0\ \mathrm{ms}$. How long must the input be held for the capacitor voltage to come within $1.0\%$ of its final value, in seconds?
solution: The error decays as $e^{-t/\tau}$, so we need $e^{-t/\tau} = 0.010$, i.e. $t = \tau\ln 100$. With $\tau = 2.0\ \mathrm{ms}$, $t = 2.0\times10^{-3}\times4.605 = 9.21\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Charge sharing loss
statement: A $10\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor is charged to $100\ \mathrm{V}$ and then connected, through a resistor, in parallel with an identical uncharged $10\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor. Find the total energy dissipated in the resistor by the time the transient ends, in joules.
solution: Charge is conserved, so the final common voltage is $50\ \mathrm{V}$. The energy drops from $\tfrac12(10\ \mu\mathrm{F})(100)^2 = 0.0500\ \mathrm{J}$ to $2\times\tfrac12(10\ \mu\mathrm{F})(50)^2 = 0.0250\ \mathrm{J}$, and the missing $0.0250\ \mathrm{J}$ is heat, regardless of $R$.

name: Heat in the first time constant
statement: A $200\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor is charged from zero through a resistor by a $50\ \mathrm{V}$ battery. Find the energy dissipated in the resistor between $t=0$ and $t=\tau$, in joules.
solution: The resistor current is $I = (V_0/R)e^{-t/\tau}$, so $W_R = \int_0^{\tau} I^2R\,dt = \frac{CV_0^2}{2}\left(1-e^{-2}\right)$. With $\tfrac12 CV_0^2 = 0.250\ \mathrm{J}$, $W_R = 0.250(1-0.1353) = 0.216\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Capacitor bridging two dividers
statement: A $12\ \mathrm{V}$ battery drives two parallel branches. The left branch is $R_1 = 1.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ from the positive terminal to node $A$, then $R_2 = 1.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ from $A$ to the negative terminal. The right branch is $R_3 = 2.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ from the positive terminal to node $B$, then $R_4 = 3.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ from $B$ to the negative terminal. A $47\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor joins $A$ and $B$. Find the magnitude of the final voltage across the capacitor, in volts.
solution: At steady state no current crosses the capacitor, so each branch is an undisturbed divider: $V_A = 12(1/2) = 6.0\ \mathrm{V}$ and $V_B = 12(3/5) = 7.2\ \mathrm{V}$. The capacitor voltage magnitude is $|V_A - V_B| = 1.20\ \mathrm{V}$.

name: Time constant across a bridge
statement: In the same network — a $12\ \mathrm{V}$ battery with a left branch $R_1 = 1.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ to node $A$ then $R_2 = 1.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ to the negative terminal, a right branch $R_3 = 2.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ to node $B$ then $R_4 = 3.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ to the negative terminal, and a $47\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor between $A$ and $B$ — find the time constant of the capacitor transient, in seconds.
solution: Replace the battery by a wire; then the two terminals merge, so from $A$ the pair $R_1\|R_2 = 500\ \Omega$ is seen, and from $B$ the pair $R_3\|R_4 = 1200\ \Omega$, in series through the capacitor. Thus $R_{th} = 1700\ \Omega$ and $\tau = (1700)(4.7\times10^{-5}) = 0.0799\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: When the power drops to a quarter
statement: A $470\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor charged to $60\ \mathrm{V}$ discharges through a $1.5\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor. Find the time at which the instantaneous dissipated power has fallen to one quarter of its initial value, in seconds.
solution: Since $P \propto e^{-2t/\tau}$, a factor of $1/4$ requires $e^{-2t/\tau} = 1/4$, i.e. $t = (\tau/2)\ln 4 = \tau\ln 2$. With $\tau = 0.705\ \mathrm{s}$, $t = 0.489\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Equalisation time constant of two capacitors
statement: A $12\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor charged to some voltage is connected through a $2.2\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor to an uncharged $4.0\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor, forming a single loop. Find the time constant with which the voltages equalise, in seconds.
solution: The transferred charge sees the two capacitors in series, since the same current flows through both. The effective capacitance is $(12)(4)/(16) = 3.0\ \mu\mathrm{F}$, so $\tau = (2200)(3.0\times10^{-6}) = 6.60\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Charge then short
statement: At $t=0$ an uncharged $100\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor begins charging through a $10\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor from a $20\ \mathrm{V}$ battery. At $t = 1.0\ \mathrm{s}$ the battery is instantaneously replaced by a plain wire, leaving the capacitor to discharge through the same resistor. Find the capacitor voltage at $t = 2.0\ \mathrm{s}$, in volts.
solution: The time constant is $\tau = RC = 1.00\ \mathrm{s}$ in both phases. At $t=1.0\ \mathrm{s}$ the capacitor has reached $V_1 = 20(1-e^{-1}) = 12.64\ \mathrm{V}$, which is the initial condition for the discharge. One more time constant later, $V = 12.64\,e^{-1} = 4.65\ \mathrm{V}$.

name: Two capacitors opposing in a loop
statement: A $100\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor charged to $50\ \mathrm{V}$ is connected in a single series loop with an uncharged $50\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor and a $300\ \Omega$ resistor, so that the charged capacitor drives current into the uncharged one. Find the total energy dissipated in the resistor, in joules.
solution: Current stops when the two capacitor voltages oppose and cancel: $(Q_0-q)/C_1 = q/C_2$ gives $q = Q_0C_2/(C_1+C_2) = 1.667\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{C}$, so both end at $33.33\ \mathrm{V}$. The initial energy $0.1250\ \mathrm{J}$ falls to $\tfrac12(100\,\mu\mathrm{F}+50\,\mu\mathrm{F})(33.33)^2 = 0.0833\ \mathrm{J}$, so $0.0417\ \mathrm{J}$ is dissipated.

name: Equivalent resistance of a balanced bridge
statement: A Wheatstone bridge runs from node $P$ to node $Q$. Arm $PA = 100\ \Omega$, arm $AQ = 200\ \Omega$, arm $PB = 300\ \Omega$, arm $BQ = 600\ \Omega$, and a galvanometer of $50\ \Omega$ connects $A$ to $B$. Find the resistance between $P$ and $Q$, in ohms.
solution: The bridge is balanced because $100/200 = 300/600$, so $A$ and $B$ are at the same potential and the galvanometer carries no current — remove it. The two arms $300\ \Omega$ and $900\ \Omega$ are then in parallel: $R = (300)(900)/1200 = 225\ \Omega$.

name: Balancing a bridge
statement: In a Wheatstone bridge from $P$ to $Q$, arm $PA = 300\ \Omega$, arm $AQ = 450\ \Omega$, and arm $PB = 120\ \Omega$. Find the value of arm $BQ$ that makes the galvanometer between $A$ and $B$ read zero, in ohms.
solution: Zero galvanometer current means $R_{PA}/R_{AQ} = R_{PB}/R_{BQ}$. Solving, $R_{BQ} = R_{AQ}R_{PB}/R_{PA} = (450)(120)/300 = 180\ \Omega$.

name: Cube across a body diagonal
statement: Twelve identical $6.0\ \Omega$ resistors form the edges of a cube, one resistor on each edge. Find the resistance measured between two opposite corners of the cube, in ohms.
solution: Symmetry puts the three corners next to the input at one potential and the three next to the output at another, so the path splits into three parallel, then six parallel, then three parallel resistors: $R = R_0(1/3+1/6+1/3) = (5/6)R_0$. With $R_0 = 6.0\ \Omega$, $R = 5.0\ \Omega$.

name: Cube across one edge
statement: Twelve identical $6.0\ \Omega$ resistors form the edges of a cube. Find the resistance measured between the two ends of a single edge, in ohms.
solution: The standard symmetry result for an edge measurement is $R = (7/12)R_0$. With $R_0 = 6.0\ \Omega$, $R = 3.5\ \Omega$.

name: Cube across a face diagonal
statement: Twelve identical $12\ \Omega$ resistors form the edges of a cube. Find the resistance measured between two corners that lie on the same face but are diagonally opposite on that face, in ohms.
solution: For a face diagonal the symmetry result is $R = (3/4)R_0$. With $R_0 = 12\ \Omega$, $R = 9.0\ \Omega$.

name: An infinite ladder
statement: An infinite ladder is built from identical $2.0\ \Omega$ resistors: a series resistor along the top rail, then a shunt resistor across the rails, then another series resistor, another shunt, and so on forever. Find the input resistance of the ladder, in ohms.
solution: Cutting off the first section leaves an identical infinite ladder, so $X = R + \frac{RX}{R+X}$ with $R = 2.0\ \Omega$. This gives $X^2 - RX - R^2 = 0$, so $X = R(1+\sqrt5)/2 = 3.24\ \Omega$.

name: Delta of three resistors
statement: Three identical $9.0\ \Omega$ resistors are connected in a triangle (delta) between terminals $A$, $B$, and $C$. Find the resistance between $A$ and $B$, in ohms.
solution: One resistor sits directly between $A$ and $B$; the other two are in series ($18\ \Omega$) and in parallel with it. So $R = (9)(18)/27 = 6.0\ \Omega$.

name: Delta to Y conversion
statement: Three identical $30\ \Omega$ resistors form a delta between terminals $A$, $B$, and $C$. Find the resistance of each arm of the equivalent Y (star) network, in ohms.
solution: The delta-Y formula for arm $A$ is $R_A = R_{AB}R_{CA}/(R_{AB}+R_{BC}+R_{CA})$. For a symmetric delta this reduces to $R_Y = R_\Delta/3 = 10\ \Omega$.

name: Square across a diagonal
statement: Four identical $8.0\ \Omega$ resistors form a square loop $A\!-\!B\!-\!C\!-\!D\!-\!A$. Find the resistance between the opposite corners $A$ and $C$, in ohms.
solution: Two paths run from $A$ to $C$: through $B$ and through $D$, each $16\ \Omega$. In parallel these give $R = 16/2 = 8.0\ \Omega$.

name: A bridge resistor that carries nothing
statement: From node $P$ to node $Q$ there are two branches: $P\!-\!A$ is $100\ \Omega$ and $A\!-\!Q$ is $200\ \Omega$; $P\!-\!B$ is $150\ \Omega$ and $B\!-\!Q$ is $300\ \Omega$. A $75\ \Omega$ resistor connects $A$ to $B$. Find the resistance between $P$ and $Q$, in ohms.
solution: The ratios match ($100/200 = 150/300$), so $A$ and $B$ sit at equal potential and the $75\ \Omega$ bridging resistor carries no current. The remaining branches are $300\ \Omega$ and $450\ \Omega$ in parallel: $R = (300)(450)/750 = 180\ \Omega$.

name: Current through an unbalanced bridge
statement: A $6.0\ \mathrm{V}$ battery is connected between $P$ and $Q$. Arm $PA = 100\ \Omega$, arm $AQ = 200\ \Omega$, arm $PB = 300\ \Omega$, arm $BQ = 400\ \Omega$, and a galvanometer of resistance $50\ \Omega$ connects $A$ to $B$. Find the magnitude of the current through the galvanometer, in amperes.
solution: The bridge is unbalanced ($100/200 \neq 300/400$), so write node equations at $A$ and $B$ with $V_P = 6.0\ \mathrm{V}$ and $V_Q = 0$. Solving gives $V_A = 4.099\ \mathrm{V}$ and $V_B = 4.000\ \mathrm{V}$, so $I = (V_A-V_B)/50 = 1.98\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{A}$.

name: Resistance of an unbalanced bridge
statement: Arm $PA = 100\ \Omega$, arm $AQ = 200\ \Omega$, arm $PB = 300\ \Omega$, arm $BQ = 400\ \Omega$, and a $50\ \Omega$ resistor connects $A$ to $B$. Find the resistance between $P$ and $Q$, in ohms.
solution: The bridge is unbalanced, so no series-parallel reduction works; use a delta-Y transform on $P\!A\!B$ or solve the node equations directly. Injecting $1\ \mathrm{A}$ at $P$ and extracting it at $Q$ gives $V_P - V_Q = 208.6\ \mathrm{V}$, so $R = 208.6\ \Omega$.

name: Strain gauge bridge output
statement: A strain-gauge bridge has all four arms equal to $350.00\ \Omega$ and is driven by a $5.00\ \mathrm{V}$ supply across the bridge. Straining one gauge raises its resistance to $350.35\ \Omega$. Find the resulting open-circuit output voltage between the two midpoints, in volts.
solution: For a small change in one arm, the output of an initially balanced bridge is $V_{out} \approx V\,\Delta R/(4R)$. Here $V_{out} = 5.00(0.35)/(4\times350) = 1.25\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{V}$.

name: Ladder with unequal rungs
statement: An infinite ladder has $4.0\ \Omega$ series resistors along the top rail and $6.0\ \Omega$ shunt resistors across the rails, repeating forever. Find the input resistance, in ohms.
solution: Self-similarity gives $X = 4 + \frac{6X}{6+X}$, i.e. $X^2 - 4X - 24 = 0$. The positive root is $X = 2 + \sqrt{28} = 7.29\ \Omega$.

name: A three-section ladder
statement: A finite ladder has three sections. Starting from the input: a $4.0\ \Omega$ series resistor, then a $6.0\ \Omega$ shunt, then a $4.0\ \Omega$ series, a $6.0\ \Omega$ shunt, a $4.0\ \Omega$ series, and a final $6.0\ \Omega$ shunt, with nothing beyond. Find the input resistance, in ohms.
solution: Work inward from the far end. The last section is $4+6 = 10\ \Omega$; then $4 + (6\|10) = 7.75\ \Omega$; then $4 + (6\|7.75) = 7.38\ \Omega$.

name: Octahedron between opposite vertices
statement: Twelve identical $12\ \Omega$ resistors form the edges of a regular octahedron (six vertices, each joined to four others; only the two opposite vertices are not directly joined). Find the resistance between two opposite vertices, in ohms.
solution: By symmetry the four equatorial vertices all sit at the same potential, so they can be merged into one node. That leaves four resistors in parallel from the input to that node and four more in parallel to the output: $R = 12/4 + 12/4 = 6.0\ \Omega$.

name: Current in one edge of a cube
statement: Twelve identical $1.0\ \Omega$ resistors form a cube. A current of $1.0\ \mathrm{A}$ is fed into corner $A$ and drawn out of the opposite corner $G$. Find the current in one of the three edges meeting at $A$, in amperes.
solution: The three edges at $A$ are equivalent under the symmetry that permutes them, so they must share the input current equally. Each carries $1.0/3 = 0.333\ \mathrm{A}$.

name: Battery across a cube
statement: Twelve identical $3.0\ \Omega$ resistors form a cube, and a $6.0\ \mathrm{V}$ battery of negligible internal resistance is connected across two opposite corners. Find the total current delivered by the battery, in amperes.
solution: The body-diagonal resistance is $(5/6)R_0 = 2.5\ \Omega$. Then $I = V/R = 6.0/2.5 = 2.40\ \mathrm{A}$.

name: Hexagon ring across opposite vertices
statement: Six identical $6.0\ \Omega$ resistors are joined end to end into a closed hexagonal ring with vertices $1$ through $6$. Find the resistance between vertices $1$ and $4$, in ohms.
solution: The ring splits into two arcs from $1$ to $4$, each containing three resistors, so each arc is $18\ \Omega$. In parallel, $R = 18/2 = 9.0\ \Omega$.

name: Hexagon ring across adjacent vertices
statement: Six identical $6.0\ \Omega$ resistors form a closed hexagonal ring. Find the resistance between two adjacent vertices, in ohms.
solution: The two arcs joining adjacent vertices are one resistor ($6\ \Omega$) and five resistors ($30\ \Omega$). In parallel, $R = (6)(30)/36 = 5.0\ \Omega$.

name: Another unbalanced bridge
statement: Arm $PA = 10\ \Omega$, arm $AQ = 20\ \Omega$, arm $PB = 30\ \Omega$, arm $BQ = 15\ \Omega$, and a $25\ \Omega$ resistor joins $A$ to $B$. Find the resistance between $P$ and $Q$, in ohms.
solution: Since $10/20 \neq 30/15$ the bridge is unbalanced, so convert the delta $P\!A\!B$ to a Y or solve the node equations. Feeding $1\ \mathrm{A}$ from $P$ to $Q$ gives a potential difference of $17.18\ \mathrm{V}$, so $R = 17.18\ \Omega$.

name: Square with a diagonal brace
statement: Five identical $20\ \Omega$ resistors are arranged as a square loop $A\!-\!B\!-\!C\!-\!D\!-\!A$ plus one extra resistor connecting $B$ to $D$. Find the resistance between $A$ and $C$, in ohms.
solution: The network is symmetric under swapping $B$ and $D$, so those two nodes sit at the same potential and the diagonal brace carries no current. The remaining two paths $A\!-\!B\!-\!C$ and $A\!-\!D\!-\!C$ are $40\ \Omega$ each, giving $R = 20\ \Omega$.

name: Infinite grid, adjacent nodes
statement: An infinite square grid of nodes is built so that every nearest-neighbour pair is joined by an identical $8.0\ \Omega$ resistor. Find the resistance between two adjacent nodes, in ohms.
solution: Use superposition: inject $I$ at node $A$ and let it escape to infinity, so each of the four edges at $A$ carries $I/4$; separately extract $I$ at the neighbour $B$, which also puts $I/4$ in the joining edge. Superposing, the $A\!-\!B$ edge carries $I/2$, so $V_{AB} = (I/2)R_0$ and $R = R_0/2 = 4.0\ \Omega$.

name: Cube with a broken edge
statement: Twelve identical $10\ \Omega$ resistors form a cube with corners $A$ and $G$ opposite. One edge meeting at corner $A$ is then cut open, leaving eleven resistors. Find the resistance between $A$ and $G$, in ohms.
solution: The full three-fold symmetry is broken, but the mirror symmetry exchanging the two surviving edges at $A$ survives, which pairs up nodes and reduces the network to a small series-parallel chain. Solving the node equations gives $R_{AG} = (11/10)R_0 = 11.0\ \Omega$, up from $(5/6)R_0 = 8.33\ \Omega$ for the intact cube.

name: Power in the galvanometer
statement: A $6.0\ \mathrm{V}$ battery is connected between $P$ and $Q$ of a bridge with arms $PA = 100\ \Omega$, $AQ = 200\ \Omega$, $PB = 300\ \Omega$, $BQ = 400\ \Omega$ and a $50\ \Omega$ galvanometer between $A$ and $B$. Find the power dissipated in the galvanometer, in watts.
solution: Solving the two node equations gives $V_A - V_B = 0.0992\ \mathrm{V}$ across the galvanometer. Then $P = (V_A-V_B)^2/R_g = (0.0992)^2/50 = 1.97\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{W}$.

name: Two-by-three resistor mesh
statement: A rectangular mesh has six nodes in two rows of three. Every horizontally adjacent pair and every vertically adjacent pair is joined by an identical $10\ \Omega$ resistor (seven resistors in all). Find the resistance between the top-left node and the bottom-right node, in ohms.
solution: There is no balanced bridge here, so solve the node equations (or exploit the $180^\circ$ rotational symmetry about the mesh centre, which relates the two measurement nodes). Injecting $1\ \mathrm{A}$ across the diagonal gives $14.0\ \mathrm{V}$, so $R = 14.0\ \Omega$.

name: Attenuation down a ladder
statement: An infinite ladder has $1.0\ \Omega$ series resistors along the rail and $2.0\ \Omega$ shunt resistors across the rails. A current $I_0$ enters the input. Find the ratio of the current in the third shunt resistor to $I_0$. Answer as a dimensionless number.
solution: Self-similarity gives $X = 1 + 2X/(2+X)$, whose positive root is $X = 2.0\ \Omega$. At each node the current therefore splits between a $2\ \Omega$ shunt and a remaining ladder that also looks like $2\ \Omega$, so exactly half the arriving current goes into each shunt. Hence the shunts carry $I_0/2, I_0/4, I_0/8$, and the third ratio is $0.125$.

name: Infinite capacitor ladder
statement: An infinite ladder is built from identical $2.0\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitors: a series capacitor along the top rail, a shunt capacitor across the rails, another series capacitor, another shunt, and so on. Find the input capacitance, in farads.
solution: Let $X$ be the input capacitance. Removing one section leaves the same ladder, so $X$ is the series combination of $C$ with the parallel pair $(C + X)$: $X = C(C+X)/(2C+X)$, giving $X^2 + CX - C^2 = 0$. The positive root is $X = C(\sqrt5-1)/2 = 1.236\ \mu\mathrm{F} = 1.236\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{F}$.

name: Infinite grid, diagonal neighbours
statement: An infinite square grid joins every nearest-neighbour pair of nodes with an identical $10\ \Omega$ resistor. Find the resistance between two nodes that are diagonal neighbours (one step across and one step up), in ohms.
solution: Superposition (inject $I$ at one node, extract $I$ at the other, and add the two single-node solutions) reduces the problem to the lattice Green function of the square grid. The standard result for a diagonal pair is $R(1,1) = (2/\pi)R_0$, which follows from the rotational symmetry of the grid about a node combined with $R(1,0) = R_0/2$. Numerically $R = (2/\pi)(10) = 6.37\ \Omega$.

name: A tapered transmission line
statement: A model transmission line is an infinite ladder whose sections grow geometrically. Section $n$ (with $n = 0, 1, 2, \dots$) has a series resistor $100\cdot 2^n\ \Omega$ along the rail followed by a shunt resistor $200\cdot 2^n\ \Omega$ across the rails. Find the input resistance at section $0$, in ohms.
solution: The ladder beyond section $0$ is an exact copy of the whole ladder with every resistance doubled, so its input resistance is $2X$. Then $X = 100 + \frac{200(2X)}{200+2X}$, which reduces to $X^2 - 200X - 100^2 = 0$ and gives $X = 100(1+\sqrt2) = 241\ \Omega$.
